klammer.etymology: Continues Middle High German klamer, klamere and Old High German klamara ('cramp-iron, clasp, hook'), a feminine tool noun derived with the -er/-ara instrument suffix from the West Germanic root *klam- ('to press together, squeeze tightly'). That same root appears in Old High German klamma ('trap, constriction, mountain gorge'), Old English clamm ('tight grip, fetter, bond'), and the causative verb klemmen ('to pinch, jam'). From its original smithing and carpentry sense of an iron cramp holding stones or timbers fast, Klammer broadened to clothespegs, paperclips, surgical staples, and—since Early New High German printing—paired typographical brackets ( ) holding parenthetical words together. English clamp (via Middle Dutch/Low German klampe) and clam belong to the same Germanic family.

cognates.meaning: clamp (< Middle Dutch klampe) and clam (< OE clamm 'tight grip') share the *klam- root

klammer.notes: One handy German noun covers everything that pinches two things together: Wäscheklammer ('clothespin'), Büroklammer ('paperclip'), Haarspange/Haarklammer ('hairclip'), and punctuation Klammern ('brackets/parentheses').

klavierduett.etymology: Musical compound combining Klavier ('piano') and Duett ('duet'), both rooted ultimately in Latin via Romance musical terminology. Klavier entered seventeenth-century German from French clavier ('keyboard', from Medieval Latin clāviārium and Classical Latin clāvis 'key', originally referring to organ, clavichord, and harpsichord manuals before specializing in eighteenth-century German to the pianoforte). Duett was borrowed in the eighteenth century from Italian duetto, diminutive of duo ('pair, piece for two', from Latin duo 'two', Indo-European cognate with German zwei and English two). In nineteenth-century domestic music-making (Hausmusik), four-handed Klavierduette became the classic way to play symphonies and dances together at home.

kompass.etymology: Kompass entered German in the 15th century (early New High German kompas, cumpas) through maritime and mercantile trade from Italian compasso 'pair of dividers, graduated circle, magnetic mariner's compass'. Italian compasso is a noun formed from Vulgar Latin *compassāre 'to pace out, measure off equally with steps', combining Latin com- 'together' and passus 'step, pace' (from pandere 'to stretch'). The meaning shifted from 'stepping off equal distances' to 'dividers for drawing circles' (still the main meaning of French compas) and finally to the round dial of the magnetic directional instrument. Modern German stresses the first syllable and writes double ss after the short vowel.
kompass.notes: Watch the false friend in geometry class: a magnetic compass for north is der Kompass, whereas a drawing compass for circles is der Zirkel!

Latin complēre combines intensive com- ('together, thoroughly') with the root verb *plēre ('to fill', seen in plēnus 'full'), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- ('to fill'). Through Grimm's law (*p- > *f-), that same Indo-European root yielded native Germanic voll ('full', Proto-Germanic *fullaz < *plh₁nós) and füllen ('to fill'), making komplett and voll distant cousins. Unlike English complete, German komplett keeps end-stress with a short lax vowel [kɔmˈplɛt].

kratzer.etymology: Kratzer is a masculine noun formed with the suffix -er from the verb kratzen 'to scratch, scrape', originally naming a person or tool that scrapes (Early New High German) and later a single scratching action or the mark left behind ('a scratch'). Kratzen continues Old High German krazzōn (9th century) and Middle High German kratzen 'to claw, scratch, scrape', from West Germanic *krattōn, with the High German consonant shift turning geminate tt into the affricate tz. Through Frankish or Middle Dutch cratten, the Germanic verb also entered Gallo-Romance as French gratter 'to scratch' and contributed to Middle English cracchen, which blended with scrat to produce modern English scratch.

kreis.etymology: Kreis continues Old High German and Middle High German kreiz 'drawn boundary line, magic circle, combat ring, district' (9th century), from West Germanic *kraita-. In the High German consonant shift, final t after a vowel shifted to the fricative spelled z in Middle High German and s today, while Dutch krijt ('combat ring, arena') kept the unshifted t. Philologists connect *kraita- with the Germanic verbal root of Old High German krizzōn 'to scratch, incise' (modern kritzeln 'to scribble'): a Kreis was originally a line scratched into the earth to mark off a judicial assembly or single-combat ring. From 'enclosed ring' arose both the geometric sense 'circle' and administrative or social senses ('district, circle of friends').

cognates.meaning: combat ring, arena (in het krijt treden)

kreis.notes: Every time you see a German county licence plate or hear Freundeskreis ('circle of friends'), you are hearing a word that once meant a line scratched in the dirt around medieval duellists.

kräutertopf.etymology: Determinative compound formed from Kräuter, the umlauted -er plural of Kraut ('herb, leafy plant', Middle High German and Old High German krūt < West Germanic *krūdą, of uncertain pre-Germanic origin; compare Dutch kruid), and masculine Topf ('pot'). Notice that German uses the plural Kräuter for culinary and medicinal herbs, whereas singular Kraut often refers to cabbage (Sauerkraut) or foliage (Unkraut 'weed').

kunst.etymology: Continues Middle High German and Old High German kunst ('knowledge, wisdom, learned skill, mastery'), a feminine verbal abstract built with the Germanic *-sti- suffix (*kun-stiz) to the preterite-present verb können ('to know how, be able', Old High German kunnan < Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, cognate with English can and cunning). Just as Macht comes from mögen and Pflicht from pflegen, Kunst originally meant 'that which one knows how to do', contrasting in medieval usage with raw strength. Only in the eighteenth century—under the influence of French les beaux-arts (die schönen Künste)—did Kunst specialize primarily to aesthetic creation while keeping everyday idioms like Das ist keine Kunst! ('Anyone can do that!').

kunstwerk.etymology: Determinative compound attested since Early New High German, uniting Kunst ('skill, art', Old High German kunst from können) and neuter Werk ('work, deed, creation'). Werk continues Middle High German werc and Old High German werk from Proto-Germanic *werką (< Proto-Indo-European *wérgom, from *werg- 'to do, make', related to Ancient Greek ergon), the exact cognate of Old English weorc and modern English work. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries Kunstwerk first denoted an ingenious mechanical contrivance, clockwork, or water-pumping engine (Wasserkunst) wrought by skilled craftsmanship, before eighteenth-century aesthetics established its modern meaning of a work of fine art.

leine.etymology: Continues Middle High German līne and Old High German līna ('cord, flaxen rope, towline'), showing regular Early New High German diphthongization of long ī to ei [aɪ̯]. Adopted early into West Germanic from Late and Medieval Latin līnea ('linen thread, plumb-line, cord', feminine substantive of līneus 'made of flax', from līnum 'flax'), alongside native Germanic derivatives of Lein ('flax'). Because cords and rigging lines were spun from tough flax fibres, the word came to denote taut household and nautical cords (Wäscheleine) as well as a dog's lead (Hundeleine). English line (blending Old English līne 'rope, cord' and Old French ligne) shares this exact history.

cognates.meaning: shares Old English līne ('rope, cord', as in clothesline) and Latin līnea

rootFamily.gloss: to put on a leash; moor

leine.notes: Notice how die Leine ('cord, clothesline') and das Leinen ('linen cloth') come from the very same flax plant—ropes and napkins were once spun from the same crop!

leinenserviette.etymology: Material compound combining Leinen ('linen fabric') and Serviette ('table napkin'). Leinen arose as the substantivized neuter of the old material adjective Middle High German līnīn, Old High German līnīn ('made of flax', derived from līn 'flax' < Latin līnum / Proto-Germanic *līną), making it the exact cognate of English linen (< Old English līnen). Serviette was borrowed in the sixteenth century into bourgeois and courtly German table culture from French serviette ('small towel or napkin presented at table', derived from servir 'to serve' < Latin servīre). Thus Leinenserviette pairs inherited Germanic household weaving vocabulary with French dining etiquette.

cognates.meaning: linen (< OE līnen) is exact cognate of Leinen; British/Commonwealth serviette comes from the same French word

leinenserviette.notes: Pronounce Serviette with a live [v] in the middle—[zɛʁˈvjɛtə]—preserving its French borrowing!

lernen.etymology: Continues Middle High German lernen and Old High German lirnēn, lernēn ('to learn, acquire by practice'), from West Germanic *liznōną, an inchoative -n- verb showing Verner's law (*-z- > West Germanic *-r-) beside the causative lehren ('to teach', Old High German lēran < Proto-Germanic *laizijaną 'to make know'). Both trace back to a Proto-Germanic preterite-present *lais ('I have tracked out, I know') and ultimately to Proto-Indo-European *leys- ('furrow, track', preserved in German Gleis 'railway track' and Latin līra 'plough-furrow')—so 'learning' originally meant 'following a track step by step'. Old English leornian (> English learn) and lǣran (> lore) preserve this exact Germanic verb pair.

lieblingstee.etymology: Compound formed with the productive German prefixoid Lieblings- ('favourite') and Tee ('tea'). Liebling ('darling, favourite', attested since the seventeenth century and parallel in formation to English darling) combines lieb ('dear, beloved', Middle High German liep, Old High German liob < Proto-Germanic *leubaz, cognate with English lief and love) with the personal suffix -ling; joined by genitive -s-, Lieblings- became German's standard equivalent of English 'favourite X' (Lieblingsbuch, Lieblingstee). Tee entered seventeenth-century German via Dutch thee (imported by the Dutch East India Company) from Hokkien/Amoy Min Nan tê, the coastal Fujian pronunciation that gave Western Europe both German Tee and English tea (as opposed to Mandarin chá > Russian čaj).

cognates.meaning: lieb is cognate with love/lief; tea shares the Dutch/Hokkien maritime trade route

lieblingstee.notes: German has no common standalone adjective for 'favourite'—instead, snap Lieblings- onto the front of any noun: Lieblingstee, Lieblingsfilm, Lieblingsplatz!

loch.etymology: Continues Middle High German and Old High German loh ('hidden place, cave, dungeon, aperture, hole') from Proto-Germanic *luką ('enclosure, opening shut by a cover or bolt'), showing the High German consonant shift of post-vocalic *-k to fricative -ch [x]. Built to the zero-grade of the strong verb Proto-Germanic *lūkaną ('to close, lock', Old High German lūhhan, Old English lūcan), its exact English cognate is lock ('fastening, canal chamber' < Old English loc). Already in Old High German the sense shifted from 'closed hiding hole or hatchway' to 'opening, perforation' generally. Notice how the plural Löcher [ˈlœçɐ] automatically shifts from back velar [x] (ach-Laut after o) to palatal [ç] (ich-Laut after front umlauted ö).

cognates.meaning: exact phonetic cognate (< OE loc < PGmc *luką), which kept the older 'enclosure/fastening' sense
obsolete/dialectal Dutch lok ('hole, bore') matches Loch

loch.notes: Das Loch [lɔx] vs die Löcher [ˈlœçɐ] is the classic showcase pair for German's two ch-sounds: back ach-Laut after a/o/u, soft ich-Laut after ä/ö/ü/e/i!

locker.etymology: Attested since late Middle High German and Early New High German, where East Central German extended locker ('porous, slack, not tight') gradually replaced shorter Upper German luck, lück ('full of gaps or pores', Middle High German lücke). It derives with expressive West Germanic gemination (*-kk-) from the same Proto-Germanic *luk- root seen in Loch ('hole') and Lücke ('gap, breach' < Old High German lucka). Originally describing crumbly garden soil, spongy bread, or slackly twisted rope ('full of little air-spaces'), locker broadened to wobbly screws, untaut cords, and—in twentieth-century colloquial German—an easygoing, relaxed attitude (locker bleiben), alongside the idiom eine Schraube locker haben ('to have a screw loose').

morphemes.meaning: characteristic of adjectives like wacker, tapfer

cognates.meaning: shares the underlying Germanic *luk- root with Loch and Lücke

locker.notes: Helpful nuance: eine lockere Schraube is still in the wood—just wobbly and needing a turn—whereas loses Papier isn't attached to anything at all.

lose.etymology: Entered standard High German chiefly from Middle Low German and East Central German lōs, lōse ('unfastened, detached, unbound'), an inflected doublet of native High German los (Middle High German and Old High German lōs 'free from, devoid of', preserved uninflected in Was ist los?, loslassen, and privative -los as in endlos). Both descend from Proto-Germanic *lausaz ('free, loose, empty'), formed to the strong verb *leusaną ('to lose, release', preserved with rhotacism in German verlieren < *farleusaną) from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- ('to untie, sever'). Notably, English loose was itself borrowed from Old Norse lauss (replacing Old English lēas, which survived only as the suffix -less), making German lose and English loose close Germanic cognates.

morphemes.meaning: Low/Central German adjectival ending distinguishing lose from predicate los

cognates.meaning: loose (< Old Norse lauss) and -less (< OE lēas) both reflect PGmc *lausaz

lose.notes: Notice the neat split in modern German: attributive lose keeps final -e (loses Papier, loser Tee), while predicate/prefix los drops it (Der Hund ist los! / loslassen).

losgehen.etymology: Losgehen combines the separable prefix los- 'loose, free, off' with gehen 'to go, walk', attested in this inchoative sense ('to set off, get started') since Early New High German. The adjective los continues Old High German lōs 'free, released' and Proto-Germanic *lausaz (cognate with English loose and the suffix -less), from the image of untying a tether or releasing a hound or carriage. Once the rope is 'loose', movement begins.

history.meaning: to come loose; to set off, begin

cognates.meaning: to come loose; to get going

losgehen.notes: On its own at the start of a race or walk, Los! means 'Off we go!' — literally 'Released!'.

loslassen.etymology: Separable compound verb attested since Middle High German (lōs lāzen 'to set free, release from bonds'), univerbating predicate los- ('free, released', Old High German lōs < Proto-Germanic *lausaz) with strong verb lassen ('to let, allow, leave'). Lassen continues Middle High German lāzen and Old High German lāzan from Proto-Germanic *lētaną ('to let, leave behind, slacken'), showing the High German consonant shift of post-vocalic *-t- to voiceless fricative -ss- [s], directly cognate with Old English lǣtan > modern English let. Thus loslassen is the exact etymological mirror of English 'to let loose' (Norse-derived loose + native let). Unlike modal-like bare lassen after infinitives, loslassen always forms its past participle with -ge- (hat losgelassen).

history.meaning: to release from captivity or grip

cognates.meaning: both elements are exact Germanic cognates (let < OE lǣtan < PGmc *lētaną)

loslassen.notes: Watch a subtle spelling detail in 2nd-person plural present of lassen: ihr lasst los (no umlaut in ihr!), whereas 2nd/3rd singular have umlaut: du lässt los, er lässt los.

minze.etymology: Minze continues Old High German minza (8th/9th century, alongside munza) and Middle High German minze 'mint'. Together with Old English minte (modern English mint), it was borrowed early into West Germanic through Roman and monastic herb cultivation from Latin menta 'mint'. Because the borrowing occurred early enough to undergo the High German consonant shift of post-consonantal t to the affricate z [ts], German has Minze where English kept mint. Latin menta itself comes from Ancient Greek mintha or minthē, widely considered a pre-Greek Mediterranean substrate word for the aromatic plant.
minze.notes: Wait — why did Latin moneta ('coin, mint') give German Münze ('coin') while Latin menta gave Minze ('mint herb'), whereas English merged both into mint? High German kept their vowels apart!

German mirrored this split by adopting feminine die Mode for fashion and trend alongside scholarly masculine der Modus for procedure or grammatical mood.

mond.etymology: Continues Middle High German māne (later mānde, mōnde), Old High German māno, from Proto-Germanic *mēnō ('moon'). Ultimately it reflects Proto-Indo-European *meh₁nōs ('moon, month'), built on the verbal root *meh₁- ('to measure'), naming the moon as the heavenly measurer of time.

nieseln.notes: Notice how diminutive -eln turns rain into gentle mist: Es regnet ('It's raining') vs. Es nieselt ('It's drizzling').

nirgends.etymology: Continues Middle High German niergen, niergent ('nowhere'), extended in Early New High German with an excrescent dental -d- after -n- and the adverbial genitive suffix -s (compare abends and teils). Middle High German niergen goes back to Old High German nio wergin ('never anywhere, nowhere at all'), univerbating nio ('never', from ni 'not' + io 'ever') with the spatial adverb wergin ('anywhere, somewhere'). Wergin matches Old Saxon hwergin and Old English hwergen, built on the Proto-Germanic interrogative-indefinite stem *hʷa- ('where, who').
nirgends.notes: Nirgends and nirgendwo mean the exact same thing ('nowhere'), just like Dutch nergens; nirgends is slightly shorter and punchier in spoken German.

noch.etymology: Old High German noh and Middle High German noch combined nu ('now') with an enclitic particle meaning 'also, and', yielding 'even now, still, yet'.

sources.title: DWDS: noch

norden.etymology: Norden continues Old High German nordan 'from the north', an adverb of direction that came to be used as a noun; the simple form appears in OHG nord and Middle High German nort. Both go back to Proto-Germanic *nurþ- 'north', shared by all the Germanic languages. The deeper origin is uncertain: a frequent suggestion links it to an Indo-European root *ner- 'below, left', as in Greek nérteros 'lower', since north lies to the left when one faces the rising sun. The same -en adverb pattern explains Süden, Osten and Westen.
norden.notes: French nord and Spanish norte were borrowed from Old English or Old Norse; the compass points in many European languages are Germanic.

notizbuch.etymology: Modern determinative compound of Notiz ('written note, memorandum') and Buch ('book'), formed in the 18th–19th centuries for a pocket pad or bound jotter. Notiz entered German via chancery and commercial Latin nōtitia ('knowledge, acquaintance, official record, list'), derived from nōtus ('known'), past participle of nōscere ('to come to know'). Buch continues Middle High German buoch, Old High German buoh, from Proto-Germanic *bōks ('inscribed tablet, book'), traditionally linked to Buche ('beech tree') on whose smooth wood runes were carved.

cognates.meaning: observation, announcement (< Old French < Latin nōtitia)
bound volume (< Old English bōc, cognate with Buch)

notizbuch.notes: Das Notizbuch always means a paper notebook for writing by hand; for a laptop computer, German borrows English das Notebook or says der Laptop.

nummerieren.etymology: Nummerieren was formed in the 16th–17th century as a commercial and chancery verb from Latin numerāre 'to count, number' (or Italian numerare), adapted to the German noun Nummer 'number' with the loan suffix -ieren. Latin numerus 'number, division' goes back to an Indo-European root *nem- 'to allot, distribute'. Until the 1996 German spelling reform the verb was written numerieren with one m, even though Nummer already had two.
nummerieren.notes: Like studieren and probieren, verbs ending in -ieren stress the ending and skip ge- in the past: nummeriert.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: nummerieren

nummeriert.etymology: Lexicalized past participle of nummerieren ('to assign sequential numbers'), formed with the loan-verb suffix -ieren on Nummer ('number') alongside Italian numerare and Latin numerāre ('to count, number'). Nummer entered Early New High German in the 16th century through South German trade with Italy, adapting Italian mercantile numero ('number', written before bale and invoice figures), from Latin numerus ('number, count, division'). Modern German writes double mm in Nummer and nummeriert to reflect the short vowel [ʊ] of the noun.

cognates.meaning: arithmetical count (< Old French nombre < Latin numerus)

nummeriert.notes: Notice why nummeriert has no ge- prefix: all German verbs ending in unstressed-stem -ieren form their past participle without ge-.

oberfläche.etymology: Oberfläche is a compound of ober 'upper' and Fläche 'flat area'. It is attested from the 18th century and is generally explained as a loan translation of Latin superficies, itself from super 'above' and facies 'face, form'. Fläche goes back to Middle High German vlæche and Old High German flahhī, an abstract noun from the adjective flach 'flat'. Ober is the comparative-like form of the adverb ob 'above', related to English over.

cognates.meaning: same structure via French, from Latin superficies

oberfläche.notes: Oberfläche and English surface are built the same way: 'over' + 'face/flat side', one from German parts, one from Latin ones.

oho.etymology: An expressive double interjection uniting the exclamation o! with ho!, attested across German dialogue since at least Early New High German. oje.etymology: Everyday German exclamation attested since Middle High German (oiē, ochē) and Early New High German (o je), combining the interjection o! with je!. While partly rooted in spontaneous expressive vocalization, je! became widespread in Early New High German as a veiled, euphemistic shortening of Jesus! (compare Herrje! from Herr Jesus! and o jemine! from Latin o Jesu Domine!), avoiding taking a sacred name in vain in casual speech. That blend of natural sigh and minced oath parallels English gee! and gosh!.
oje.notes: Stress falls on the second syllable with a long vowel (o-JEH [oˈjeː]), never on the initial o-.

orange.etymology: German Orange was borrowed from French orange in the 17th century, partly through Dutch, and first referred to the fruit; the colour adjective followed. French orange goes back via Old Italian (n)arancia and Arabic nāranj to Persian nārang, and ultimately to Sanskrit nāraṅga, probably of Dravidian origin. The initial n- was lost in the Romance languages by false division (una narancia read as un'arancia), and the vowel o- was likely influenced by French or 'gold' or the town name Orange. The older German word Pomeranze comes from the same Italian source, while Apfelsine means 'apple from China'.
orange.notes: Spanish naranja still has the original n- that French, English and German lost.

orangenschale.etymology: "Orangenschale" is a determinative compound consisting of the noun "Orange" (orange) and "Schale" (peel, shell). "Orange" was borrowed into German in the 17th century from French "orange", which traces back via Spanish and Arabic to Persian "nārang" and Sanskrit "nāraṅga". "Schale" derives from Middle High German "schale" and Old High German "scala", meaning shell, husk, or drinking vessel. The Old High German term goes back to Proto-Germanic "*skalō", related to the root for dividing or splitting. The English cognates include "orange" and "shell".
orangenschale.notes: Notice the linking "-n-" often found when forming compounds with feminine nouns ending in "-e".

osten.etymology: Osten continues Old High German ōstan 'from the east', an old directional adverb beside the shorter noun ōst (Middle High German ōsten), just like Norden, Süden and Westen. It goes back to Proto-Germanic *austra- / *austanē 'east, from the east', derived from the Proto-Indo-European dawn goddess and 'shining dawn' root *h2ews- (compare Latin aurōra and Greek ēōs). 'East' is thus literally the direction of the morning sunrise, and the spring festival Ostern (Easter) shares the same dawn root.

history.meaning: from the east, in the east

osten.notes: Osten, Ostern (Easter) and Österreich (Austria, 'eastern realm') all grow from the ancient root for the morning dawn.

packpapier.etymology: "Packpapier" is a determinative compound of the verb stem "pack-" (from "packen", to pack) and the noun "Papier" (paper). The verb "packen" originates from Middle High German "packen", related to Middle Low German "pakken" and eventually to a widespread Germanic root for bundles. "Papier" entered Middle High German as "papier" from Old French "papier" and Latin "papyrus", ultimately from Ancient Greek "papyros" referring to the papyrus plant. This paper was typically robust and used for wrapping or packing goods.
packpapier.notes: Combines a verb stem directly with a noun, a common pattern for materials meant for an action.

papierschiff.etymology: Determinative compound joining Papier ('paper', Late Middle High German papīr < Latin papȳrus < Ancient Greek pápyros) with Schiff ('ship, vessel'). Schiff continues Middle High German schif, Old High German skif, from Proto-Germanic *skipą ('boat, hollowed vessel'), showing the regular High German consonant shift of postvocalic *-p to -ff (contrast unshifted English ship and Dutch schip). Once inexpensive paper and newsprint entered everyday homes in the 19th century, Papierschiff (and diminutive Papierschiffchen) became the standard name for a folded toy boat.
papierschiff.notes: German Schiff and English 'ship' are exact twins separated by the High German consonant shift (*-p > -ff), just like Affe/'ape' and offen/'open'.

parkbank.etymology: "Parkbank" is formed from the nouns "Park" (park) and "Bank" (bench). The word "Park" was adopted into German in the 18th century from English "park" and French "parc", both ultimately from Medieval Latin "parricus" meaning an enclosed space. "Bank" comes from Middle High German "banc" and Old High German "banch", which goes back to Proto-Germanic "*bankiz". The Germanic root is thought to be related to the Indo-European base "*bheg-" meaning to break or bend, initially referring to a raised earthwork.
parkbank.notes: The plural forms of "Bank" differ by meaning: "Bänke" for benches, "Banken" for financial institutions.

partner.etymology: The word "Partner" was borrowed into German in the 19th century from English "partner". The English term evolved from Middle English "partener", an alteration of "parcener", which derives from Old French "parçonier" (joint heir). This Old French word is rooted in Latin "partitio", a division or sharing, from the verb "partiri" (to divide). Thus, a partner fundamentally denotes someone who shares in an activity, enterprise, or relationship.
partner.notes: In modern German, it is broadly used for business associates, dance partners, or spouses.

passieren.etymology: Borrowed via Middle Low German passēren and 16th-century Early New High German from French passer ('to step across, pass by, elapse; reflexively se passer = to happen, occur'), fitted with the German suffix -ieren. French passer descends from Vulgar Latin *passāre ('to step, pace, cross'), formed from Latin passus ('step, pace', originally a participial noun to pandere 'to stretch out the legs'). Remarkably, German absorbed both the spatial French verb ('to pass a gate or border') and the reflexive event sense ('to happen'), neatly telling them apart by auxiliary: haben for crossing a place, sein for happening.

morphemes.meaning: step, pass, occur (< French passer < Latin passus)

history.meaning: to cross, pass / to take place

cognates.meaning: to go by, cross; come to pass (< Old French passer)
to pass; se passer = to happen

passieren.notes: Think of English 'come to pass': Was ist passiert? ('What happened?') is one of the highest-frequency conversational sentences in German.

Because the Latin word entered Germanic before the High German consonant shift, both p sounds shifted regularly: initial p- became affricate pf- and postvocalic -p- became fricative -ff- (compare unshifted English pipe and Dutch pijpen from the very same Latin source). Originally a weak verb, pfeifen crossed into the strong Class I pattern (pfeifen – pfiff – gepfiffen) in Late Middle High German on the model of greifen.

rahmen.etymology: "Rahmen" is derived from Middle High German "rame" and Old High German "rama", meaning a support, frame, or loom. The word is of Germanic origin, tracing back to Proto-Germanic "*ramō", which denoted a post, pillar, or prop. The modern verb "rahmen" (to frame) is formed directly from this noun. Historically, it referred to wooden structures used for weaving or stretching cloth, evolving into the modern sense of a picture frame or conceptual framework.
rahmen.notes: This is the verb "to frame", distinct from the noun "der Rahmen" which shares the same spelling.

rangehen.etymology: Colloquial separable verb shortened by apheresis of unstressed he- from herangehen ('to step up to, approach'), joining ran- (< heran = her 'hither' + an 'at, onto') with gehen ('to go, walk'). Gehen continues Middle High German gēn / gān, Old High German gēn / gān, from West Germanic *gāną / *gēną, ultimately reflecting Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁- ('to step forth, leave'). With 20th-century household telephones, ans Telefon rangehen—and elliptically just rangehen—became the standard spoken German idiom for answering a ringing call.

morphemes.meaning: up to, to it (shortened from heran)

history.meaning: to approach; to answer the phone/door

cognates.meaning: to move, walk (< Old English gān, cognate with gehen)

rangehen.notes: Spoken German drops the initial he- in many directional compounds: heran > ran (rangehen), herein > rein (reinkommen), heraus > raus (rausgehen).

rasch.etymology: "Rasch" goes back to Middle High German "rasch" and Old High German "rasc", meaning quick, swift, or agile. The word originates from Proto-Germanic "*raskaz" (quick, fast). This adjective belongs to a wide Germanic word family, with cognates in Old English ("ræsc", lightning) and Old Norse ("röskr", vigorous). The root is likely related to concepts of movement and energy, resulting in the English word "rash" for hasty actions.
rasch.notes: A slightly more elevated or literary synonym for "schnell" (fast).

rascheln.etymology: Attested since Early New High German in the 16th century, rascheln is formed with the iterative verb suffix -eln ('to do repeatedly in small movements') on an onomatopoeic stem rasch- imitating dry friction. Related dialectal raschen ('to rustle, rush') and Middle High German rasch ('brisk, crisp') belong to the same expressive West Germanic sound group. Its morphological build closely parallels English rustle (Middle English rustlen) and Dutch ritselen, where a sibilant followed by -l- iconically evokes the light crinkling of dry leaves, straw, or paper.

cognates.meaning: to make soft dry sounds (parallel West Germanic -l- formation)

rascheln.notes: Notice the German suffix -eln (rascheln, klingeln, tröpfeln, lächeln), which regularly expresses small, light, or repeated actions—just like English -le in 'rustle', 'crackle', and 'trickle'.

regenwolke.etymology: Ancient West Germanic determinative compound attested already in Old High German reganwolka and Middle High German regenwolke, joining Regen ('rain') with Wolke ('cloud'). Regen continues Old High German regan from Proto-Germanic *regną ('rain'), while Wolke continues Middle High German wolke, Old High German wolka / wolkan from Proto-Germanic *wulkną ('cloud', related to *welk- 'moist, damp'). Old English possessed the exact compound regnwolcen, though English later replaced wolcen ('welkin') with cloud.

reif.etymology: "Reif" evolved from Middle High German "rīfe" and Old High German "rīfi", meaning mature or ready for harvest. It stems from Proto-Germanic "*rīpijaz", meaning mature or ready to be reaped. The root is historically connected to verbs for harvesting or plucking, such as the Old English "rīpan" (to reap). Thus, the core concept denotes a fruit or crop that has reached the point of being ready for collection and consumption.

revers.etymology: "Revers" was borrowed into German in the 18th century from French "revers" (the back side, lapel). The French word comes from Latin "reversus", the past participle of "revertere" (to turn back). In tailoring terminology, the "Revers" is the part of a jacket or coat collar that is folded back on the chest. The term initially meant the reverse side of a coin before shifting focus to the turned-back lapels of clothing.
revers.notes: Pronounced with stress on the second syllable and a silent or spoken 's' depending on dialect and plural form.

rezept.etymology: Rezept comes from Medieval Latin receptum 'what has been received', the neuter past participle of Latin recipere 'to take, receive' (re- + capere 'to take'). It entered German in the 16th century as a medical term for a doctor's written instruction, because such instructions traditionally began with the imperative recipe 'take!', still abbreviated Rp. on prescriptions. From the pharmacy the word spread to cooking, and the sense 'cooking recipe' became common in the 18th century. English kept two separate developments: recipe from the imperative and receipt from the participle.
rezept.notes: Rezept and Rezeption are from the same Latin verb: the front desk 'receives' guests, the recipe tells you what to 'take'.

ring.etymology: Ring is an inherited Germanic word: Old High German (h)ring and Middle High German rinc go back to Proto-Germanic *hringaz 'circle, ring', with the initial h- lost in German as in many hr- words. It is found across Germanic, for example Old Norse hringr and Old English hring. Outside Germanic it is usually compared with Old Church Slavonic krǫgŭ 'circle', pointing to an Indo-European root meaning 'to bend, turn'. A Frankish form *hring was borrowed into French as rang 'row, rank', which German later borrowed back as Rang.
ring.notes: Rang (rank) and arrangieren took a detour through French but come from the same Frankish word for ring.

rings.etymology: "Rings" is an adverb derived from the noun "Ring" (circle, ring) by appending the adverbial genitive suffix "-s". The noun "Ring" comes from Middle High German "rinc" and Old High German "hring", stemming from Proto-Germanic "*hringaz" (circle, ring). The form "rings" emerged in the Early Modern German period to express the idea of "in a circle" or "all around", and it is frequently used in the fixed expression "rings um" (all around).
rings.notes: Usually found in combinations like "ringsum" or "ringsherum" to mean "all around".

ritzen.etymology: Ritzen continues Middle High German ritzen and Old High German rizzōn 'to scratch, incise, cut lines into', an intensive geminated formation beside the strong verb reißen 'to tear, draw'. It goes back to West Germanic *writtōn, from Proto-Germanic *wrītaną 'to scratch runes, carve, write', which is the direct source of English write. Before ink and paper, writing in the Germanic world meant scratching letters into wood or stone.
ritzen.notes: German ritzen ('to scratch into stone or wood') preserves the ancient physical action behind English 'write'.

roh.etymology: Continues Middle High German rō (inflected stem rāw-, rōw-), Old High German rō, rāo, from Proto-Germanic *hrawaz ('raw, uncooked, untreated'), with early loss of initial h- before r- and New High German silent -h marking vowel length and bridging the hiatus in inflected forms like rohes. It is the exact cognate of English raw (< Old English hrēaw), Dutch rauw, and Old Norse hrár. All trace back to Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- ('raw flesh, clotted blood'), the same root behind Latin crūdus ('raw, rough' > English crude) and Ancient Greek kréas ('meat').
roh.notes: Just like English 'raw', German roh covers both uncooked food (rohes Ei) and natural, unvarnished materials (rohes Holz, rohe Seide).

rucksack.etymology: "Rucksack" is an Alemannic and Austro-Bavarian compound word that entered standard German in the 19th century. It combines "Ruck-" (from "Rücken", meaning back) and "Sack" (sack or bag). The first element is a dialectal variant of "Rücken", descending from Middle High German "rücke" and Old High German "hrukki". The second element, "Sack", comes from Middle High German "sac" and Latin "saccus", ultimately a borrowing from Greek and Semitic sources. English borrowed the word from German in the late 19th century.
rucksack.notes: This Alpine regional word successfully replaced other terms for back-carried bags and was loaned into English.

ruhe.etymology: Continues Middle High German ruowe, ruo ('rest, repose, quiet, calm'), Old High German ruowa, from Proto-Germanic *rōwō ('calm, stillness, rest'). Between Middle and New High German the diphthongs monophthongized (uo > ū) and intervocalic -w- disappeared, while orthographic -h- remained as a vowel-length and syllable-boundary sign in Ruhe [ˈʁuːə]. It matches Old English rōw ('quiet, rest') and Old Norse ró ('calm, peace'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- ('to rest, be still'), a close relative of the dental stem behind German Rast and English rest.

cognates.meaning: rest, calm (from the closely related dental derivative)

rustikal.etymology: Borrowed into scholarly and aesthetic German in the 18th–19th centuries from Late/Medieval Latin rūsticālis ('belonging to the country, rural'), an extension in -ālis of Classical Latin rūsticus ('rural, country-bred, plain'). Latin rūsticus derives in turn from rūs, rūris ('open countryside, farmstead'), cognate with English rural. Whereas older literary usage sometimes echoed Classical Latin's contrast between urbane refinement and 'rustic' roughness, modern German interior style and gastronomy use rustikal warmly for honest, solid craftsmanship in natural timber, stone, and coarse grain.

rührung.etymology: "Rührung" (emotion, sentiment) is derived from the verb "rühren" (to stir, to touch emotionally) and the suffix "-ung". The verb comes from Middle High German "rüeren" and Old High German "hruorēn" (to set in motion, touch), from Proto-Germanic "*hrōzijaną" (to stir). Originally referring purely to physical movement or stirring (like stirring a pot), the metaphorical sense of moving someone's feelings developed strongly during the 18th century period of Sentimentalism.
rührung.notes: Often used to express being emotionally moved or touched by a gesture.

sand.etymology: Sand is inherited from Proto-Germanic *sanda-, found as Old High German and Middle High German sant, Old English sand and Old Norse sandr. Most etymologists derive it from an Indo-European root *bhes- 'to rub, grind', via a form *bhsamdho-. The same root is seen in Greek psámmos 'sand' and possibly Latin sabulum 'coarse sand'. The meaning 'ground, crushed material' fits the idea of rock rubbed into grains.

sauer.etymology: Sauer continues Old High German and Middle High German sūr 'sour, bitter, harsh', from Proto-Germanic *sūraz. In the transition to New High German the long ū regularly became the diphthong au, exactly as in hūs to Haus. Related words outside Germanic include Lithuanian sūrus 'salty' and Old Church Slavonic syrŭ 'raw, damp', pointing to an Indo-European adjective for a sharp taste. The colloquial sense 'annoyed' (sauer sein) is a figurative extension of the 'sour' face of an annoyed person.
sauer.notes: Sauerstoff (oxygen) is a calque of French oxygène, 'acid-maker', because chemists once believed oxygen was the essence of all acids.

In sentences like Es ist schade ('It is a loss/harm -> It's a shame'), the predicate noun froze without the oblique -n that remodeled modern der Schaden!

schade.notes: Because schade began life as a noun ('a loss'), it can NEVER stand attributively before a noun (*eine schade Sache is ungrammatical); it is used only predicatively (Das ist echt schade!) or alone (Schade!).

schatz.etymology: "Schatz" descends from Middle High German "schaz" and Old High German "scaz", initially meaning a coin, money, or wealth. This traces back to Proto-Germanic "*skattaz" (coin, treasure). The original meaning was likely associated with cattle as a medium of exchange, akin to Old Frisian "sket" (cattle, money). Over time, the meaning generalized to signify any hoard of valuables, and eventually became a widespread term of endearment for a loved one.
schatz.notes: Besides physical treasure, it is the most common German term of endearment for a partner.

schatzkarte.etymology: Schatzkarte is a modern compound of Schatz 'treasure' and Karte 'map'. Schatz goes back to Old High German scaz and Middle High German schaz 'coin, money, wealth', from Proto-Germanic *skatta-, compare Gothic skatts 'coin' and Old English sceatt 'money'; its further origin is unclear. Karte was borrowed in the 15th century from French carte and Latin charta 'sheet of papyrus', from Greek chártēs. The specialised sense 'map' developed from 'sheet', as in Landkarte.
schatzkarte.notes: Schatz is also a term of endearment (mein Schatz = my darling), and schätzen 'to value, estimate' comes from it.

schaukeln.etymology: Early New High German iterative verb in -eln formed alongside die Schaukel ('swing') from older schuckeln and schauken ('to rock, swing to and fro'). These go back to Middle High German schocken, schucken ('to swing, dance, jolt, thrust') and Old High German scoc ('swinging motion'), a West Germanic stem also found in Middle Dutch schocken ('to jolt, shake'). With expressive diphthongization to schau- and the frequentative -eln suffix, schaukeln specialized for smooth, rhythmic rocking on water, ropes, or a garden swing.

scherzen.etymology: "Scherzen" (to joke, jest) comes from the noun "Scherz" (joke). The noun derives from Middle High German "scherz" (joyful leaping, jest), which belongs to the verb "scherzen" (to leap merrily, to joke). This word family originates from a Germanic root expressing lively, jumping movements, related to Old High German "scerzōn" (to leap about). The transition from physical leaping to verbal joking occurred in the medieval period, reflecting playful behavior.
scherzen.notes: Used for making jokes or not being serious, for instance "Ich scherze nur" (I am only joking).

schicht.etymology: Schicht was taken into standard German from Low and Central German, where it is attested in late medieval mining language as schicht 'division, row, layer, work period'. The -cht is the northern development of earlier -ft (compare Low German-derived Schacht beside Schaft), so the word corresponds to a form *schift 'division'. It belongs with Middle Low German schiften and English shift, originally 'to divide, arrange', from Proto-Germanic *skiftijan-. The mining senses 'layer of rock' and 'work shift' both come from the idea of a section or allotted part.

cognates.meaning: work shift; to move (orig. to divide, arrange)

schicht.notes: Schicht and English shift are cousins: the miners' working day was 'divided' into shifts, and the rock into layers.

schleifen.notes: Fascinating verb split! Craft/woodworking schleifen ('to sand wood, sharpen knives, cut gems') is STRONG (schliff, hat geschliffen), whereas 'to drag along the floor / tie a bow' (from die Schleife) is WEAK (schleifte, hat geschleift)!

schleifpapier.etymology: Determinative compound of the stem of schleifen ('to grind, whet, sand smooth', MHG slīfen, OHG slīfan) and Papier ('paper', Late MHG papīr), denoting sandpaper.

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schleifpapier

schlicht.etymology: Continues Middle High German sliht ('smoothed out, flat, plain, straightforward'), variant with i-vocalism beside OHG sleht / MHG sleht (< Proto-Germanic *slihtaz 'smooth, level', cognate with English 'slight').

cognates.meaning: from the same Proto-Germanic *slihtaz ('smooth, plain -> slender')

rootFamily.gloss: to smooth over, mediate a dispute

schlicht.notes: Fascinating twin history: schlicht and schlecht started as variants of the exact same word meaning 'smooth, plain'—schlicht kept the positive sense 'gracefully simple', while schlecht drifted to 'poor, bad'!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schlicht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schlicht

schließen.etymology: From Middle High German sliezen and Old High German sliozan ('to slide a bolt, lock, shut, conclude'), strong verb from Proto-Germanic *sleutaną (distantly related to Latin claudere 'to close' from PIE *(s)kleh₂w- 'hook, peg, key').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schließen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schließen

schließlich.etymology: Early New High German adjective and adverb (16th century) formed with -lich from the stem of schließen ('to close, lock, conclude, infer', MHG sliezen, OHG sliozan < Proto-Germanic *sleutaną), originally meaning 'conclusive, by way of final conclusion' before developing both temporal ('finally, eventually') and justificatory ('after all') uses.

cognates.meaning: finally; after all (showing the exact same semantic duality from the cognate verb sluiten 'to close')
borrowed via Middle Dutch/Low German from the same *sleutaną ('bar, bolt') root

schließlich.notes: Pay close attention to word stress and context: narrative schließlich means 'eventually, at last', whereas explanatory schließlich appeals to shared obvious knowledge — 'after all!' (Das hier ist schließlich Altona! 'This IS Altona, after all!').

Wiktionary: schließlich (German)

schlimm.etymology: From Middle High German slimp (inflected slimber, 'slanted, crooked, awry, bad'), from West Germanic *slimba- ('oblique, crooked'); shifted semantically from 'crooked, askew' to 'unwelcome, bad, severe'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schlimm
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schlimm

schloss.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive Schloss (OHG sloz, MHG sloz) from schließen ('to lock, shut', OHG sliozan); it meant first a bolt or lock and later a locked fortification or palace.

history.meaning: to shut, bolt -> door lock, bolt
lock, clasp; fortified stronghold locking a valley or pass
mechanical lock; stately palace or chateau

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Middle Dutch/Low German slot ('bar, bolt, hollow')

schloss.notes: Why are a 'padlock' and 'Neuschwanstein Palace' the same word (das Schloss, pl. die Schlösser)? Because a medieval fortress 'locked' a strategic road or pass — later evolving into a royal palace (while fortified ruins stay die Burg)!

schluck.etymology: From Middle High German sluck ('gulp, swallow, mouthful of liquid'), deverbal noun from schlucken ('to swallow, gulp', MHG slucken, from Middle Low German slūken).

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schluck

schluss.etymology: Middle High German sluz ('locking, conclusion'), verbal abstract from schließen ('to close, conclude').

history.meaning: act of locking shut, keystone of an arch, conclusion

cognates.meaning: lock; ending (tot slot = German zum Schluss)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schluss
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schluss

schluss.notes: Sibling ablaut noun to das Schloss: der Schluss (pl. die Schlüsse) means 'closing / end' — Zum Schluss ('finally / at the end'), Schluss für heute! ('That's a wrap for today!').

schlussakkord.etymology: Compound of Schluss ('closing, end, conclusion', MHG sluz, verbal noun from schließen 'to close, lock') and Akkord ('musical chord, harmony', borrowed in the 17th century from French accord < Vulgar Latin *accordāre 'to bring into harmony, tune strings together', from cor 'heart').

history.meaning: final resolving chord of a composition

cognates.meaning: Schluss shares the root of 'slot'; Akkord = 'accord/chord'

schlussakkord.notes: Since the 1996 spelling reform, Schluss is written with double s (ss) instead of ß because its vowel u is short.

schlüssel.etymology: Old High German sluzzil and Middle High German slüzzel were formed with the instrument suffix *-ila from schließen (OHG sliozan 'to lock, bolt'), literally 'the locker / opener'.

schmal.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German smal ('small, slender, narrow, scarce'), from Proto-Germanic *smalaz, exact cognate of English 'small' (which generalized to size, whereas German narrowed to width).

schmecken.etymology: From Middle High German smecken, smacken and Old High German smecken, smackēn ('to have a flavor, taste, perceive by taste or smell'), from West Germanic *smakkjan- / *smakēn-, cognate with English 'smack' (a taste).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schmecken
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schmecken

schnappen.etymology: Entered standard German via Late Middle High German snappen from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch snappen ('to snatch, snap with the jaws, gasp, chatter'), acquiring regular High German palatalization of initial sn- to schn- [ʃn]. Notably, the unshifted medial geminate -pp- (where native Upper German had schnapfen) betrays its Low German origin, just like klappen and schleppen. Originally sound-symbolic of jaws or a latch snapping shut, it broadened in everyday German to catching something in mid-air or quickly grabbing a coat.

history.meaning: to snap with the jaws, snatch

cognates.meaning: to bite/catch sharply (borrowed from Middle Dutch/Low German snappen)

rootFamily.gloss: to pick up (a word or rumour)

schnappen.notes: Unshifted -pp- in German (schnappen, Treppe, Ebbe/Krabbe-type coastal/northern loans) is a classic clue that a word travelled south from Low German.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: schnappen
Wiktionary: schnappen (German)

schneeweiß.etymology: Elative color compound from Middle High German snēwīz and Old High German snēwīz ('white as snow'), combining Schnee ('snow', OHG snēo) and weiß ('white', OHG hwīz).

cognates.meaning: English 'board' and German Brett are related by r-metathesis (< *bordą / *bredą)

schneidebrett.notes: German builds kitchen gear directly from action + object: schneiden + Brett = das Schneidebrett ('cutting board'), backen + Blech = das Backblech ('baking sheet').

schneiden.etymology: From Middle High German snīden and Old High German snīdan ('to cut, carve, reap, tailor'), strong verb from Proto-Germanic *snīþaną, cognate with Old English snīþan.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schneiden

schnell.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German snel ('vigorous, brave, agile, swift'), from Proto-Germanic *snellaz ('active, bold, quick', borrowed into Italian as snello), cognate with Old English snell ('keen, quick').

schnellzug.etymology: "Schnellzug" (express train) is a determinative compound consisting of the adjective "schnell" (fast) and the noun "Zug" (train, pull). "Schnell" derives from Old High German "snel" (brave, quick, agile) and Proto-Germanic "*snellaz". "Zug" stems from Middle High German "zuc", related to the verb "ziehen" (to pull, draw). In the 19th century, with the advent of railways, the word was coined to describe trains that traveled faster and made fewer stops than local passenger trains.
schnellzug.notes: An older term for an express train; today, acronyms like ICE (Intercity-Express) are more common.

schnur.etymology: Continues Old High German snuor and Middle High German snuor ('cord, twine, string, lace'), from Proto-Germanic *snōrō ('twisted cord'), from the PIE root *sneh₁- ('to spin, twist thread', cf. nähen 'to sew').

cognates.meaning: related Germanic cord-word (< Old English sneare / Old Norse snara 'noose, cord')

schnur.notes: From die Schnur comes the verb schnüren ('to lace up shoes or a parcel') and the everyday word for shoelaces, die Schnürsenkel!

schonen.notes: Doctor's-order German at its most useful: 'Sie müssen Ihren Fuß schonen!' means 'You must rest / stay off your foot!'.

schraube.etymology: From Late Middle High German schrūbe ('threaded metal bolt or wood screw'), borrowed via MiddleFrench escroue ('female screw, nut') from Medieval Latin scrōfa ('sow; screw-nut', by metaphorical comparison with a rooting pig or sow's tail).

schrauben.etymology: Schrauben was derived in Early New High German (15th–16th century) from the noun die Schraube 'screw' (late Middle High German schrūbe). Schraube was borrowed via Middle French escroue 'nut, female screw' (modern French écrou), which itself goes back to Latin scrōfa 'breeding sow' in Roman craftsmen's slang metaphor for an interlocking socket and threaded spindle. English screw came from the same Old French workshop term.

cognates.meaning: screw; to fasten with a screw (via Old French)

schrauben.notes: Both German Schraube and English screw trace back to the same medieval French craftsmen's word escroue.

schwellung.etymology: Action and result noun in -ung formed from the strong verb schwellen ('to swell, expand', OHG swellan, MHG swellen < Proto-Germanic *swellaną).

cognates.meaning: exact root and suffix cognate (swell + -ing = schwell + -ung)!

schwellung.notes: English 'swelling' and German die Schwellung match piece for piece: swell = schwell-, and English -ing corresponds to German feminine -ung!

schön.etymology: From Middle High German schœne and Old High German scōni ('shining, bright, fair, beautiful'), originally a verbal adjective meaning 'worth looking at, notable' from Proto-Germanic *skaunijaz, derived from the root of schauen ('to look, behold'). Cognate with English 'sheen'.

schönen.etymology: Inflected form (notably masculine accusative singular in elliptical wishes like Schönen Tag noch! '[Have a] nice day!') of schön ('beautiful, lovely, nice'), continuing Middle High German schœne and Old High German scōni ('shining, bright, splendid, fair to behold'), a verbal adjective from Proto-Germanic *skauniz built on the root of schauen ('to look at, behold': literally 'worth looking at')!

morphemes.meaning: masculine accusative singular (or dative plural / weak) ending

history.meaning: visible, shining, fair to look upon

cognates.meaning: exact cognate! Old English scīene ('beautiful, bright') survives in modern English noun sheen ('lustrous glow')
clean (in the Netherlands); beautiful (in Flanders/southern Dutch)

rootFamily.gloss: to look (derived from the same *skauw- 'gaze' root)
to treat gently, spare (umlautless verb twin of schön!)

schönen.notes: Why is it Schönen Tag noch! with accusative -en? Because it elliptically omits Ich wünsche dir/Ihnen einen ... ('[I wish you a] nice rest of your day!'), leaving the direct-object accusative ending intact!

schönschrift.etymology: "Schönschrift" (calligraphy, fine handwriting) is formed from the adjective "schön" (beautiful) and the noun "Schrift" (writing, script). "Schön" stems from Old High German "skōni" (shining, beautiful) and Proto-Germanic "*skauniz". "Schrift" goes back to Old High German "scrift" and Proto-Germanic "*skriftiz", which itself is an early borrowing from Latin "scriptum" (written thing). The compound designates the practice or product of writing neatly and aesthetically.
schönschrift.notes: Commonly associated with primary school exercises where children learn cursive and neat handwriting.

see.etymology: Continues Middle High German sē (inflected stem sēw-), Old High German sēo ('sea, lake'), from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz ('sea, expanse of water'), whose deeper pre-Germanic origin remains debated and is often considered an early northern European maritime substrate word. Old High German sēo was originally masculine for both inland lakes and oceans, though feminine forms already surfaced in Middle High German. Under the strong influence of Low German de See and Dutch de zee ('the sea'), modern German split the noun cleanly by gender: feminine die See for the open ocean, masculine der See for a lake.
see.notes: Article gender does real work here: an der See means 'at the seaside', whereas am See (an dem See) means 'by the lake'!

seemännisch.etymology: Relational adjective derived with suffix -isch and productive i-umlaut (a > ä) from der Seemann ('sailor, mariner', Middle High German sēman, Middle Low German sēman). The base compound unites See ('sea', < Proto-Germanic *saiwiz) with Mann ('man, person', Old High German man < Proto-Germanic *mann-), matching English seaman and Dutch zeeman word for word. Spreading inland with North German maritime terminology from the 17th century onward, seemännisch came to praise neat, practical sailorly skill in knots, rigging, and navigation.

history.stage: Middle High German / Middle Low German

cognates.meaning: sailor (< Old English sǣmann, exact parallel to the base noun)

seemännisch.notes: Suffix -isch regularly triggers umlaut on back-vowel stems: Mann > männisch (seemännisch), Stadt > städtisch, Sturm > stürmisch.

segelboot.etymology: Determinative compound combining Segel ('sail') with Boot ('boat'). Segel continues Middle High German segel, Old High German segal, from Proto-Germanic *seglą ('sail'), widely derived from Proto-Indo-European *sek- ('to cut', i.e. a cut piece of cloth). Boot entered High German in the 16th century via Middle Low German bōt, itself borrowed from Middle English bōt (< Old English bāt < Proto-Germanic *baitaz)—had Boot been inherited directly in High German, final *-t would have shifted to -ß.
segelboot.notes: Boot is an English-via-Low-German maritime loan into High German, which is why its final -t matches English 'boat' instead of shifting like Wasser/'water'.

segeln.etymology: Denominal verb continuing Middle High German sigelen, segelen and Middle Low German segelen ('to travel under sail'), derived from das Segel ('sail', Old High German segal < Proto-Germanic *seglą). Every maritime Germanic language formed the same verb from the noun: compare Old English seglian (> English sail), Dutch zeilen, and Old Norse sigla. Alongside literal sailing on water, modern German uses segeln vividly for anything flat or buoyant—a loose sheet of paper, a hat, or a gull—gliding on a current of air.

history.meaning: to sail; to glide through the air

cognates.meaning: to travel by sail; glide (< Old English seglian)

segeln.notes: Like fliegen, schwimmen, and fahren, segeln expresses movement through space and therefore forms its conversational past with sein: Er ist vorbei gesegelt / vorbeigesegelt.

senken.etymology: "Senken" (to lower, reduce) is a causative verb derived from the strong verb "sinken" (to sink). It originates from Old High German "senken" and Proto-Germanic "*sankwijaną" (to cause to sink). The Germanic pattern involves altering the root vowel to create a transitive verb from an intransitive one. Thus, "senken" inherently means "to make something sink".
senken.notes: This is a regular (weak) transitive verb requiring an object, whereas "sinken" is irregular and intransitive.

solange.etymology: Univerbation of the correlative phrase so lange ('as long as'), from Middle High German sō lange and Old High German sō lango, combining sō ('as, so') and the temporal adverb lange ('long').

solch.etymology: Continues Middle High German solch, solich and Old High German solīh, sulīh ('formed like this, of such a kind, such'), an ancient Proto-Germanic compound adjective *swalīkaz combining *swa ('so, thus', NHG so) and *līkaz ('body, shape, form', whence the suffix -lich and Leiche): literally 'so-shaped, having this form'!

morphemes.meaning: shape, kind, body (< OHG -līh, compressed from *līkaz)

cognates.meaning: exact cognate! Old English swilc palatalized and dropped -w- and -l- to become Middle/Modern English such (just as *hwilīkaz became German welch and English which!)

rootFamily.gloss: which (< *hwilīkaz 'how-shaped', exact interrogative twin of solch!)
so (colloquial so ein often replaces solch ein)

solch.notes: Uninflected solch precedes ein or elevated bare adjectives (solch ein Stress), while inflected solcher/solche/solches behaves like dieser (in solchen Situationen 'in situations like these').

sollen.etymology: From Old High German scolan / solan and Middle High German soln ('to owe, be obliged to'), related to Schuld ('debt, fault') and English 'shall / should'.

sommer.etymology: From Middle High German sumer and Old High German sumar ('summer'), from Proto-Germanic *sumaraz (cognate with English 'summer'), from Proto-Indo-European *semh₂- ('summer, half-year').

sommergast.etymology: Determinative compound of Sommer ('summer', OHG sumar, MHG sumer) and Gast ('guest, visitor', OHG gast, MHG gast), denoting a summer visitor or vacationer.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sommergast
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sommergast

sommersonne.etymology: "Sommersonne" is a determinative compound consisting of "Sommer" (summer) and "Sonne" (sun). "Sommer" goes back to Middle High German "sumer" and Old High German "sumar", originating from Proto-Germanic "*sumaraz". "Sonne" derives from Old High German "sunna" and Proto-Germanic "*sunnō". Both are foundational vocabulary words in the Germanic languages, rooted in Proto-Indo-European elements denoting the seasons and celestial bodies. The compound simply evokes the warmth and light of the summer season.
sommersonne.notes: A highly evocative, poetic word often used to emphasize warm, bright weather.

sonne.etymology: Continues Old High German sunna and Middle High German sunne ('sun, sunlight'), from Proto-Germanic *sunnǭ (< PIE *sóh₂wl̥), lowering u to o before double nasal in Central and New High German.

history.meaning: sun, sunshine (with Central German u > o before nn)

cognates.meaning: from the l-stem of the same heteroclite PIE *sóh₂wl̥!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sonne
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sonne

sonne.notes: Notice the regular u -> o shift before nn/mm in German vs. English: Sonne = sun, Sommer = summer, Nonne = nun, gewonnen = won, geschwommen = swum!

sonnenhof.etymology: Toponymic and architectural compound name from Sonne ('sun', OHG sunna, MHG sunne, with weak genitive/linking -n-) and Hof ('courtyard, estate, inn', OHG hof, MHG hof), literally 'sunny courtyard/inn'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sonnenhof
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sonnenhof

sonnenlicht.etymology: From Middle High German sunnenlieht ('sunlight'), a compound of Sonne ('sun', OHG sunna, MHG sunne) and Licht ('light', OHG lioht, MHG lieht).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sonnenlicht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sonnenlicht

sonnenschein.etymology: Inherited West Germanic compound continuing Middle High German sunnenschīn and Old High German sunnūnscīn ('the sun's radiance'), where the middle -en- preserves the old weak feminine genitive singular ending -ūn of OHG sunna ('of the sun'). Sonne goes back to Proto-Germanic *sunnōn (from the oblique n-stem of the Indo-European heteroclite sun word *sóh₂wl̥ / *sh₂wén-), while Schein ('light, gleam') is the old strong-verb noun to scheinen ('to shine' < Proto-Germanic *skīnaną). English sunshine joins the exact same two Germanic elements.

morphemes.meaning: historical weak feminine genitive ('of the sun')

sonnenschein.notes: That linking -n- in Sonnenschein, Sonnenblume, and Sonnenuntergang is a living fossil: in Old High German die Sonne was a weak noun whose genitive singular ended in -n (der Sonnenschein = 'the sun's shine').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: Sonnenschein
Wiktionary: Sonnenschein (German)

sonnenuntergang.etymology: Early New High German compound univerbating older Middle High German phrases such as der sunnen underganc ('the going-under of the sun'), retaining the historical weak feminine genitive ending -en- of Sonne ('sun', Old High German sunna < Proto-Germanic *sunnōn). Its head noun Untergang (Middle High German underganc, Old High German untargang 'setting of heavenly bodies, sinking') combines unter- ('under, below the horizon', < *under) with Gang ('going, course', verbal noun to gehen < *gangaz). It forms a transparent antonym pair with Sonnenaufgang ('sunrise').
sonnenuntergang.notes: In German the sun literally 'goes up' and 'goes down': Die Sonne geht auf (rises) -> Sonnenaufgang; die Sonne geht unter (sets) -> Sonnenuntergang.

sonnig.etymology: Derived from Sonne ('sun', MHG sunne, OHG sunna) with the adjectival suffix -ig (Early New High German sonnig, replacing older MHG sunneclīch 'sunny').

sonntag.etymology: From Middle High German suntac, sunnentac and Old High German sunnūntag ('Sunday'), a late West Germanic loan translation of Late Latin diēs sōlis ('day of the sun', itself calqued on Ancient Greek hēméra Hēlíou), combining sunnūn (genitive of sunna 'sun') + tag ('day').

sorge.etymology: From Middle High German sorge and Old High German sorga, sworga ('worry, grief, care, anxiety'), from Proto-Germanic *surgō ('care, sorrow', cognate with Old English sorh, English 'sorrow').

sortieren.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century as Hanseatic/South German merchant terminology from Italian sortire ('to divide into lots, classify merchandise by grade and type; originally to draw lots'), derived from Latin sors, sortis ('lot drawn in divination, share, rank, kind').

morphemes.meaning: lot, kind, grade (< Latin sors, sortis)

history.meaning: to allot, grade and separate wares by quality
to sort, arrange merchandise by type

cognates.meaning: via Old French sorte / sortir from the same Latin noun

sortieren.notes: In supermarket German, Sortiment ('product assortment') and Ware sortieren ('sorting stock on the shelves') still live right in the mercantile domain where the word entered German.

sozusagen.etymology: 17th–18th century univerbation of the parenthetical infinitival phrase so zu sagen ('so to say, to put it that way'), modeled on French pour ainsi dire and earlier Humanist Latin ut ita dicam, combining so ('thus, so', OHG sō), zu ('to'), and sagen ('to say', OHG sagēn).

history.meaning: that I may speak thus, so to speak
so to speak, as it were

cognates.word: so to say / so to speak

rootFamily.gloss: in a way, to some extent (near-synonym)

sozusagen.notes: Favorite German hedging adverb whenever a speaker introduces a bold metaphor — for instance Thorsten calling himself sozusagen der Leitwolf ('the alpha wolf, so to speak').

spalte.etymology: Old High German spalta ('cleft, division'), from spalten ('to split, divide into columns').

history.meaning: fissure, slit; vertical column of a two-column manuscript page!

cognates.meaning: woodworking term 'brittle/split wood' (and dialectal spald 'to split')

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Spalte

spalte.notes: Why is a spreadsheet or newspaper 'column' called die Spalte? Medieval scribes divided parchment pages down the middle ('split' them!) into vertical text columns! (Architectural stone columns are die Säule.)

spalten.etymology: Old High German spaltan, Middle High German spalten, from Proto-Germanic *spaldaną ('to cleave, split').

cognates.meaning: archaic/technical 'to split, cleave' (< Middle Dutch spalden)
borrowed from Middle Dutch splitten (distant cousin from the same *spel- 'cleave' family)

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): spalten

spalten.notes: Conjugates regularly weak in the past (spaltete), while keeping BOTH historical strong gespalten (especially figurative: eine gespaltene Meinung) and weak gespaltet (for physical wood: Holz gespaltet/gespalten).

spannen.etymology: Continues Middle High German spannen, Old High German spannan ('to stretch taut, draw a bow, fasten, yoke'), from Proto-Germanic *spannaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)penh₁- ('to draw, stretch, spin', the same root behind spinnen 'to spin' and Latin pendēre 'to hang'). Originally a reduplicating strong verb (OHG past spēn, participle gispannan), spannen shifted to regular weak conjugation (spannte, gespannt) in Early New High German. From literal mechanical tension in ropes, bows, and sails grew the modern figurative senses of mental suspense in Spannung and spannend ('gripping').

cognates.meaning: to stretch across; hand-span (< Old English spannan)

spannen.notes: Once you see spannen = 'stretch tight', a whole German family unlocks: Spannung ('tension/suspense'), spannend ('thrilling'), gespannt ('eager'), and sich entspannen ('to relax, slacken tension').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: spannen

sparen.etymology: Continues Old High German sparōn and Middle High German sparn ('to preserve intact, keep in reserve, save, spare'), derived from the Proto-Germanic adjective *sparaz ('thrifty, sparing').

history.meaning: to keep safe, preserve, use sparingly
to save (money, time, energy); sich etwas sparen ('save/spare oneself something')

cognates.meaning: Old English sparian ('to spare, save') is the exact cognate of German sparen!

sparen.notes: While English split 'save' (money/time) and 'spare' (someone trouble), German sparen does both jobs—including the warm teasing idiom 'Sparen Sie sich die Tränen!' ('Save your tears!').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sparen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sparen

sparstuhl.etymology: Playful German compound formed on the pattern of Sparpreis ('saver fare') or Sparmenü ('value menu'), combining verb stem spar- (from sparen 'to save money', OHG sparōn < Proto-Germanic *sparōną) with Stuhl ('chair', OHG stuol < Proto-Germanic *stōlaz).

history.meaning: chair bought as a money-saving bargain

cognates.meaning: both stems are exact Germanic cognates (sparen = 'spare'; Stuhl = 'stool')

sparstuhl.notes: In German, Spar- ('saver/discount') can be attached to almost any noun: Sparpreis ('saver fare' on German trains), Spardose ('money box'), Sparschäler ('economy vegetable peeler'), or Klara's teasing Sparstühle!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): sparen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sparen

spazieren.etymology: From Early New High German 'spazieren', borrowed in the 14th century from late Middle High German 'spatzieren' or 'spacieren'. This in turn stems from Italian 'spaziare' (to wander, roam) or Medieval Latin 'spatiari' (to take a walk, spread out). It ultimately goes back to Latin 'spatium' (space, distance). The loanword entered the language of the upper classes as an elegant term for strolling before spreading to general usage.

cognates.meaning: extent or area (from the same Latin root 'spatium')

spazieren.notes: While English 'walk' is used for mere movement, 'spazieren' specifically emphasizes walking for pleasure or leisure.

sources.title: DWDS: spazieren
Wiktionary: spazieren

spaziergang.etymology: Early New High German compound of spazieren ('to stroll, walk for pleasure', MHG spazieren, borrowed in the 14th c. from Italian spaziare < Latin spatiārī 'to walk about, promenade', from spatium 'space, walk') and Gang ('walk, gait', OHG and MHG gang).

history.meaning: to walk about, take a walk

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Spaziergang
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Spaziergang

spaziergänger.etymology: Agent noun derived from Spaziergang ('stroll, walk') / spazieren gehen ('to go for a stroll'): spazieren was borrowed in late Middle High German from Italian spaziare / Latin spatiārī ('to walk about, promenade', from spatium 'space'), and -gänger comes from Gang ('walk, gait', related to gehen).

history.meaning: to take a leisurely walk (< Lat. spatiārī)

cognates.meaning: spazieren comes from Latin spatium (> English 'space')!

spaziergänger.notes: Compare der Fußgänger ('pedestrian' walking anywhere in traffic) with der Spaziergänger ('stroller' out walking purely for pleasure and fresh air).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): spazieren
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): spazieren

spazierstock.etymology: Compound noun formed from the stem of 'spazieren' (to stroll) and 'Stock' (stick). The first element derives from Latin 'spatiari' via Middle High German 'spatzieren'. The second element, 'Stock', goes back to Old High German 'stoc' and Proto-Germanic '*stukkaz' (tree trunk, stick). The compound emerged in the early modern period as walking canes became fashionable accessories for gentlemen.
spazierstock.notes: A 'Spazierstock' was historically both a practical walking aid and a symbol of elegance.

spaß.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th century from Italian spasso ('pastime, amusement, walk, diversion', as in andare a spasso 'to go for a stroll'), deverbal noun from Italian spassare / spassarsi ('to amuse oneself, unbend'), from Late Latin expassāre, built on Latin passus ('step, pace', from pandere 'to spread out, stretch')!

cognates.meaning: learned/Romance relatives sharing Latin passus / pandere

spaß.notes: Few learners suspect that German's quintessential word for 'fun' (Viel Spaß! / Das macht Spaß!) is a Baroque-era Italian import originally meaning 'going out to stretch one's legs'!

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Spiegel

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): spielen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): spielen

spinne.etymology: Continues Middle High German spinne and Old High German spinna ('spider'), an agentive noun formed directly from the strong verb spinnen ('to spin thread', OHG spinnan, Proto-Germanic *spinnaną), naming the arachnid literally as 'the spinner (of webs)'.

cognates.meaning: from Old English spīþra (< *spinn-þrō 'spinner'), built on the exact same verb root with an instrument/agent suffix

rootFamily.gloss: to spin thread; colloquially 'to be crazy'

spinne.notes: Calling someone wie eine Spinne im Netz ('like a spider in its web') evokes an unseen boss monitoring every thread of an operation.

spitze.etymology: Spitze continues Old High German spizza (9th century) and Middle High German spitze 'sharp point, tip, mountain peak, vanguard', an abstract and concrete feminine noun derived from the adjective spitz (Old High German spizzi 'pointed, sharp'). Its West Germanic base *spitja- belongs to the same family as Spieß 'roasting spit' and English spit ('roasting rod'). From 'sharp end' developed figurative senses such as 'summit, head of a group, forefront'. In the 16th century Spitze also acquired the textile meaning 'lace', originally naming the pointed, saw-toothed trim (Zackenrand) sewn onto collars and cuffs.
spitze.notes: Colloquially, Das ist spitze! means 'That's top-notch / awesome!' — literally 'at the very peak' — and the Spitz dog breed was named in German for its pointed muzzle and ears.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: Spitze
Wiktionary: Spitze (German)

splittern.etymology: Denominative verb from Splitter ('splinter, shard', Late MHG/Middle Low German splitter), derived from the Germanic root *split- ('to split, cleave', cf. spleißen, English 'split').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): splittern
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): splittern

sprachnachricht.etymology: Modern compound of Sprache ('speech, voice, language', OHG sprāhha, MHG sprāche) and Nachricht ('message, news', 17th-c. shortening of Nachrichtung 'information to guide oneself by', from nachrichten 'to adjust/inform'), meaning 'voice message'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sprachnachricht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sprachnachricht

sprechen.etymology: From Middle High German sprechen and Old High German sprehhan ('to speak, utter, say'), from West Germanic *sprekaną (cognate with Old English sprecan, later specan > English 'speak').

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): sprechen

springen.etymology: Continues Old High German springan and Middle High German springen ('to leap, bound, burst forth'), a Class III strong verb from Proto-Germanic *springaną ('to jump, burst out') < PIE *sprengʰ- ('to move briskly, spring').

cognates.meaning: exact cognate (< Old English springan 'to leap, burst forth') with the same i–a–u ablaut (spring – sprang – sprung = springen – sprang – gesprungen)!

springen.notes: English 'spring – sprang – sprung' and German 'springen – sprang – gesprungen' have kept the exact same vowel melody for over two thousand years!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): springen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): springen

spritzen.etymology: Middle High German sprützen / spritzen ('to spurt, splash'), intensive formation to sprießen ('to sprout, burst forth').

history.meaning: to burst forth -> intensive 'to spurt, splash, squirt'

cognates.meaning: borrowed from German spritzen ('quick spray'; and Spritzer = wine + soda)
native cousin from metathesized Old English spryttan

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): spritzen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): spritzen

spritzen.notes: Gives English 'spritz' — in German kitchens ein Spritzer Zitronensaft is 'a squeeze/dash of lemon juice', while Vorsicht, es spritzt! warns of hot oil or paint splattering.

sprosse.etymology: From Middle High German sprozze, Old High German sprozzo ('sprout, shoot; ladder rung'), related to sprießen ('to sprout'), transferred from a projecting branch to a wooden rung.

cognates.meaning: plant shoot (from the same strong verb *spreutaną)

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sprosse

sprosse.notes: Picturesque transfer: a wooden rung sticking out across a ladder (Leitersprosse) or dividing windowpanes (Sprossenfenster) looked like shoots branching from a stem!

sprudelwasser.etymology: Compound of Sprudel ('bubbling spring, fizzy water', back-formed in the 18th c. from sprudeln 'to bubble, gush', related to sprühen) and Wasser ('water', OHG wazzar, MHG wazzer), denoting sparkling/carbonated water.

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sprudelwasser

spur.etymology: From Middle High German spur, spor, Old High German spor ('footprint, track, trace'), from Proto-Germanic *spurą (related to spüren 'to track, sense' and Sporn 'spur').

history.meaning: to kick with the foot, tread

cognates.meaning: animal track (borrowed via Afrikaans/Dutch spoor, exact cognate!)
heel spike (< Old English spura = German Sporn, from the same 'heel-kick' root)

rootFamily.gloss: to feel, sense (originally 'to follow a track'!)

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Spur
