spähen.etymology: From Middle High German spehen and Old High German spehōn ('to look closely, peer, spy, scout'), from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (whence Old French espier > English 'spy'), from Proto-Indo-European *spek- ('to observe, look at', cf. Latin specere).

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): spähen

spät.etymology: From Middle High German spæte (adverb spāte) and Old High German spāti ('late'), from Proto-Germanic *spēdiz ('late', cognate with Gothic spediza 'later'), from PIE *spē(y)- ('to stretch, take a long time, prosper').

spüren.etymology: Inherited from Middle High German spürn, spüren ('to follow a track, investigate, perceive') and Old High German spurien ('to track game, seek out'). It continues Proto-Germanic *spurjaną, a denominative verb formed with i-umlaut from the noun *spurą ('footprint, track', preserved in German die Spur). Originally a hunting verb meaning 'to read footprints in the earth', its sense broadened in medieval and early modern German to 'to detect, sense, feel physically or intuitively'.

morphemes.meaning: track, trace, perceive (umlauted stem of Spur)

history.meaning: to track game, trace, seek out

cognates.meaning: to follow a track, inquire (Scots speir)
to ask, learn (< Old Norse spyrja)

spüren.notes: To spüren the wind is literally to pick up its 'trail' (die Spur)—a medieval hunter's word that became everyday sensory German.

stab.etymology: Inherited from Middle High German stap (genitive stabes) and Old High German stab ('stick, rod, walking staff'), going back to Proto-Germanic *stabaz ('post, staff, rod'). The Germanic noun derives from the Indo-European verbal root *stebh- ('to prop, support, stiffen, set upright'). Because carved wooden rods served both as rune-bearing sticks and as batons of office, Stab also gave rise to Buchstabe ('letter of the alphabet') and collective Stab ('command or advisory staff').

cognates.meaning: wooden rod, pole; group of personnel (< OE stæf)

stab.notes: German Stab and English staff are exact cognates—right down to sharing both the physical meaning ('wooden rod') and the organizational one ('team of staff').

'Plan' was borrowed into German in the 17th century from French 'plan' and Latin 'planum' (flat surface). The term describes a flat visual layout or map of a city.
stadtplan.notes: Notice that 'Plan' in German translates to 'map' when referring to cities or public transit, whereas 'Landkarte' is used for geographical regions.

stadtvertrag.etymology: Compound of Stadt ('city, municipality', MHG stat) and Vertrag ('contract, treaty, agreement', Late MHG vertrac 'reconciliation, agreement', from vertragen 'to come to an agreement, settle').

stadtwappen.etymology: Compound of 'Stadt' (city) and 'Wappen' (coat of arms). 'Stadt' comes from Old High German 'stat' (place). 'Wappen' derives from Middle High German 'wafen' or 'wapen', which originally meant 'weapon'. Through a semantic shift influenced by chivalry, the term for armaments transferred to the heraldic symbols painted on shields.

cognates.meaning: arm, tool for combat (cognate to Wappen)

stadtwappen.notes: The connection between 'Wappen' (coat of arms) and 'Waffe' (weapon) reflects the medieval practice of painting heraldic symbols on shields.

staffel.etymology: Derived from Old High German 'staffal' (step of a staircase or ladder). It traces back to Proto-Germanic '*staplaz' (pillar, post). The meaning broadened from physical steps to hierarchical ranks, relay teams, and eventually to a 'season' of a television series. The modern TV sense was calqued from the idea of a series progressing in stages or steps.
staffel.notes: In everyday modern German, you will most frequently encounter 'Staffel' when discussing seasons of a television show.

staffelei.etymology: First attested in 17th-century German workshop terminology as Staffelei (Staffeley), formed from Staffel ('step, rung, notched support') with the stressed nominal suffix -ei (borrowed via Middle High German -īe from Old French -ie). The base Staffel descends from Old High German staffal and Proto-Germanic *stapulaz ('post, pillar, step'), from the root *stap- ('to step, tread'). An easel earned this name from the row of stepped peg-holes or rungs along its upright legs used to raise or lower a picture.

cognates.meaning: pillar, post (archaic); cognate with the base Staffel (< OE stapol)

staffelei.notes: While English easel comes from Dutch ezel ('little donkey' carrying a painting), German Staffelei names the stepped rungs (Staffeln) that hold the board at different heights.

stahl.etymology: Stahl continues Old High German stahal (9th century, alongside contracted stāl) and Middle High German stahel, stāl 'steel', from Proto-Germanic *stahliją or *stahlam. The word is shared across all branches of Germanic, including English steel (Old English stīele), Dutch staal, and Old Norse stál. Etymologists derive it from an Indo-European verbal stem *steh₂k- 'to stand firm, resist, be rigid' (compare Sanskrit stakati 'resists' and Old Prussian panu-staclan 'fire-steel'), naming steel as 'the firm, hardened metal' in contrast to softer wrought iron. In modern spelling the h both echoes Old High German stahal and marks the long vowel.
stahl.notes: Just as English says 'nerves of steel', German says Nerven wie Stahlseile ('nerves like steel cables') and seinen Körper stählen ('to steel/toughen one's body').

stimmt.etymology: Third-person singular present indicative (das stimmt 'that's right / true') of the weak verb stimmen ('to tune an instrument, bring into harmony, tally/add up in accounting, be correct; also to vote'), continuing Middle High German stimmen and Old High German stimmen ('to give voice, sound'), denominative from Stimme ('voice, pitch, vote', OHG stimma < Proto-Germanic *stemnō).

history.meaning: to tune musical strings in pitch -> to agree, balance (of accounts), be true
that's right!; at a checkout/restaurant: keep the change!

cognates.meaning: tunes, votes, agrees (cf. dat stemt overeen)
Old English stefn ('voice') was the exact cognate of German Stimme

rootFamily.gloss: to be right; to vote; to tune

stimmt.notes: Essential German cashier & café phrase! Handing over €10 for a €9.50 bill and saying Stimmt so! ('It tallies as is!') is the standard idiomatic way to say 'Keep the change!'.

stoffstreifen.etymology: A transparent compound of Stoff 'cloth, fabric, material' and Streifen 'strip, band, stripe'. Stoff entered High German in the 17th century via Middle Dutch stoffe 'woven fabric, material' from Old French estoffe 'cloth, equipment, material' (also the source of English stuff), which in turn is often linked to medieval Latin stuppa 'coarse flax' or Frankish *stoppōn 'to stuff'. Streifen goes back to Middle High German strīfe 'stripe, narrow band', reinforced by Middle Low German strīpe and New High German diphthongisation of long ī to ei, while English stripe kept the unshifted Low German p.
stoffstreifen.notes: English stuff once meant 'woven cloth' too (as in 'stuff gown'); German Stoff kept 'fabric' as a core meaning alongside 'substance' and 'topic'.

straff.etymology: Entered general High German in the 16th century from East Central German (including Luther's writings) in the senses 'pulled tight, taut, strict', corresponding to rare Middle High German straf. Etymologists connect it as an expressive West Germanic variant with labial final consonant alongside the guttural root seen in strack ('straight, stretched') and strecken ('to stretch', from Proto-Germanic *strakjaną). Its older links to Middle High German strāfen ('to pull tight, reprimand') remain debated in detail.

cognates.meaning: strict, severe, strong (partly influenced by High German)

straff.notes: Do not confuse straff ('taut, tight', short vowel [a]) with die Strafe ('punishment, fine', long vowel [aː]), even though both once touched on the idea of strictness.

summ.etymology: Summ is a direct onomatopoeic interjection imitating a continuous low buzzing or humming sound. It belongs directly with the verb summen (Middle High German summen 'to hum, buzz, drone'), formed from an expressive m-root imitating closed-lip humming and bee flight. Summ, summ, summ! became famous across the German-speaking world as the opening line of Hoffmann von Fallersleben's 1835 children's bee song ('Bienchen summ herum').
summ.notes: From electric apartment buzzers (der Türsummer) to honeybees, German captures every gentle buzz with summ.

'Kelle' goes back to Old High German 'kella' (trowel, ladle) and Proto-Germanic '*kaljōn', describing a hollowed or scoop-like tool.

takelage.etymology: Borrowed into Northern German maritime speech in the 17th to 18th century from Dutch takelage ('ship's rigging') and thence adopted into standard German. The Dutch word is a hybrid seafaring formation combining Middle Dutch and Middle Low German takel ('hoisting rope, pulley tackle') with the French collective noun suffix -age. The Germanic base takel probably belongs to words denoting a gripping prong or hook (compare Zacke 'prong'), from which English also borrowed nautical tackle.

takelage.notes: Like English tackle, German Takelage comes from North Sea sailing vocabulary—and lives on ashore in colloquial sich auftakeln ('to get all dolled up like a full-rigged ship').

teil.etymology: Teil continues Old High German and Middle High German teil 'part, portion, share, lot' (attested as both masculine and neuter from the beginning), from Proto-Germanic *dailiz and *dailą. Its exact English cognate is deal (Old English dǣl 'part, share', surviving in 'a great deal' and 'deal out cards'), showing the regular High German shift of d to t alongside German ei versus English ea from Germanic *ai. In modern standard German the old double gender settled into a semantic distinction: der Teil denotes an integrated part or section of a whole (der erste Teil), whereas das Teil denotes a loose piece, component, or item (das Ersatzteil).

For centuries it belonged chiefly to chancery, philosophical, and commercial German in expressions like Totalsumme ('grand total'). During the 20th century, uninflected total spread rapidly in colloquial spoken German as an emphatic degree adverb ('completely, really'), much like English totally.

traum.etymology: Traum continues Old High German and Middle High German troum 'dream, vision' (8th/9th century), from Proto-Germanic *draumaz. Remarkably, Old English drēam meant 'joy, music, noisy revelry', whereas Old Saxon, Old High German, and Old Norse draumr meant 'sleeping vision', a sense English dream absorbed under Scandinavian influence in the Middle Ages. Most philologists derive *draumaz (via *draugmaz, with loss of g before m) from the Germanic verb *dreuganą 'to deceive, delude' (modern German trügen, Trug), interpreting a dream originally as a deceptive phantom or illusion.
traum.notes: Träume sind Schäume ('dreams are mere foam') is a classic German proverb echoing the word's likely root in trügen ('to deceive').

The word originates from the sound-symbolic Germanic root '*tupp-' or '*tipp-', imitative of a light strike or touch. It describes the action of applying or removing liquid with light, dabbing motions.

turm.etymology: Turm goes back to Old High German turri and turn (9th to 11th centuries) and Middle High German turn, turm 'fortified tower, steeple, dungeon'. The form with final -n was borrowed through Old French torn, tor (the source also of English tower) from Latin turris (accusative turrem), itself a loan from Ancient Greek tyrsis 'walled tower'. In late Middle High German and Early New High German, final -n shifted to -m, producing modern Turm, though old n-forms survive in names like Thurn und Taxis. In chess, der Turm denotes the piece English calls the rook or castle.

rootFamily.gloss: to pile up; (coll.) to bolt, flee

turmuhr.notes: The transition of 'Uhr' from meaning 'hour' to the physical 'clock' measuring the hour reflects a common semantic shift in European languages.

umstellen.etymology: Separable verb combining the prefix 'um-' (around, re-) with 'stellen' (to place, put). 'Stellen' derives from Old High German 'stellen' and Proto-Germanic '*stallijaną' (to place). The prefix 'um-' indicates a change of position or rearrangement. Together, the verb indicates moving an object to a new location or reorganizing an arrangement.

cognates.meaning: compartment for an animal (from the same root as stellen)

umstellen.notes: As a separable verb, 'umstellen' meaning 'to shift/move' splits in the present tense: 'Ich stelle das Gepäck um'. Note that there is an inseparable version meaning 'to surround'.

umweg.etymology: Umweg goes back to Middle High German umbewec 'roundabout path, detour', a compound of the preposition and adverb um 'around, about' and Weg 'way, road, path'. Um continues Old High German umbi and Middle High German umbe, from Proto-Germanic *umbi and Proto-Indo-European *h₂mbʰi 'around, on both sides' (cognate with Greek amphi and Latin ambi-). Weg continues Old High German and Middle High German wec 'road, journey', from Proto-Germanic *wegaz, the exact cognate of English way and Dutch weg, built on *weganą 'to move, carry'. Alongside the literal road sense, figurative phrases like auf Umwegen ('indirectly') and ohne Umwege ('straight to the point') have been established since Early New High German.
umweg.notes: Watch the pronunciation contrast: the noun der Weg ('way') and der Umweg ('detour') have a long e [veːk], whereas the adverb weg ('away, gone') has a short e [vɛk]!

unglück.etymology: Derived from 'Glück' (luck, happiness) with the negating prefix 'un-'. 'Glück' stems from Middle High German 'gelücke', which initially meant the way things close or turn out, later specializing to 'good fortune'. The negative prefix creates the direct antonym, denoting misfortune, an accident, or disaster.

cognates.meaning: fortune (borrowed from Dutch, related to Glück)

unglück.notes: Depending on context, 'Unglück' can mean a minor mishap or a major tragic accident.

uni.etymology: Uni is a colloquial clipping (Kopfwort) of die Universität 'university', originating in 19th- and 20th-century student slang and now standard in everyday spoken German across Germany, Austria, and Switzerland; it retains the feminine gender of the full word (die Uni, plural die Unis). Universität itself was borrowed in the 14th century — as the earliest central European universities were founded in Prague (1348), Vienna (1365), and Heidelberg (1386) — from Medieval Latin ūniversitās, short for ūniversitās magistrōrum et scholārium 'the whole guild of masters and students'. Classical Latin ūniversitās 'totality, corporation' derives from ūniversus 'all together, turned into one' (ūnus 'one' + versus, from vertere 'to turn').
uni.notes: German loves two-syllable -i clippings that keep the original noun's gender: die Uni (die Universität), der Kuli (der Kugelschreiber), das Navi (das Navigationsgerät).

verdrehen.etymology: Continues Middle High German verdrejen, verdræjen and Old High German firdrāen ('to twist, turn awry'), combining the inseparable prefix ver- ('out of alignment, amiss') with drehen ('to turn, rotate'). The base verb descends from Old High German drāen and Proto-Germanic *þrēaną ('to twist, turn'), from Indo-European *terh₁- ('to rub, turn, bore'). From the physical sense of twisting a cord or ankle came figurative idioms for rolling one's eyes or distorting someone's words.

verehrt.etymology: Lexicalized past participle of verehren ('to revere, honour, hold in high esteem'), attested since Middle High German verēren ('to honour, bestow a respectful gift upon'). It combines the intensifying inseparable prefix ver- with ehren ('to honour', Old High German ērēn), a denominative verb derived from Ehre (Old High German ēra < Proto-Germanic *aizō 'honour, respect, awe'). Since the 18th century, verehrt has been a staple of polite salutations and respectful introductions.

cognates.meaning: honour, mercy, grace (cognate with base Ehre)

verehrt.notes: In German letters, sehr geehrte Damen und Herren is standard business style, whereas sehr verehrte Gäste sounds warmer, more ceremonial, and slightly old-world.

With reflexive sich, ver- expresses two curved edges or handles catching tightly on one another so that they cannot slide apart freely.

verheddert.etymology: Lexicalized past participle of verheddern ('to tangle, snarl up'), which spread into standard High German in the 18th and 19th centuries from Low German and Central German dialects. It combines inseparable ver- ('into disorder, entangled') with dialectal heddern ('to fray, snarl'), most plausibly derived from Middle Low German hēde ('tow, coarse tangled flax or hemp fibres combing off a distaff'). Something verheddert is thus knotted up like uncombed flax tow.

cognates.meaning: coarse flax or hemp fibres (< OE heordan, cognate with Low German Hede)

rootFamily.gloss: to get tangled; to trip over one's words

verheddert.notes: In everyday German, sich verheddern works both for lantern cords in the wind and for a speaker who gets tangled up mid-sentence!

verkauf.etymology: From Middle High German verkouf ('sale, selling'), deverbal noun from verkaufen ('to sell', MHG verkoufen, OHG firkoufen).

verkaufen.etymology: From Middle High German verkoufen and Old High German firkoufen ('to trade away, sell'), formed with prefix ver- (OHG fir- 'away, off') and kaufen ('to trade, buy, bargain', OHG koufōn, from Latin caupō 'wine-merchant, innkeeper').

verknoten.etymology: Derived in New High German by prefixing inseparable ver- ('together, tightly, into a snarl') to knoten ('to tie a knot'), a denominative verb from Knoten ('knot'). The noun continues Middle High German knote, knode and Old High German knoto, chnodo from Proto-Germanic *knudōn- ('knot, knob, joint'), belonging to a Germanic cluster of *kn- words for compact lumps and joints. While knoten means simply to tie, verknoten highlights either binding ends securely or cords knotting themselves inextricably.

history.meaning: to knot together; to become knotted

cognates.meaning: cognate with base Knoten (< OE cnotta < *knuttōn-)

verknoten.notes: Unlike English, where the k in knot fell silent centuries ago, German Knoten and verknoten pronounce both consonants crisply: [kn-].

Wiktionary: verknoten (German)

verkäufer.etymology: From Middle High German verkoufære, verköufer ('seller, merchant, vendor'), agent noun formed with suffix -er (OHG -āri) from verkaufen ('to sell', MHG verkoufen).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Verkäufer
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Verkäufer

verlassen.etymology: From Middle High German verlāzen, verlān and Old High German firlāzan ('to leave behind, abandon, release, let go; reflexively: to rely upon'), formed with prefix ver- (OHG fir-) and lassen ('to let, leave', OHG lāzan).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): verlassen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): verlassen

verlaufen.etymology: Inherited from Middle High German verloufen and Old High German firloufan ('to run away, pass by, scatter'), combining inseparable ver- ('away, astray, to completion') with the strong verb laufen ('to run'). Laufen goes back via Old High German hloufan to Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną ('to leap, run'). Depending on the subject, verlaufen expresses liquid ink running out of its lines, a road or event taking its course, or—with reflexive sich—a walker straying off the right path.

history.meaning: to bleed (ink); to proceed; (sich) to get lost

cognates.meaning: cognate with base laufen (< OE hlēapan)

verlaufen.notes: Watch the auxiliary switch: die Tinte ist verlaufen ('the ink ran', intransitive motion/change = sein), but ich habe mich verlaufen ('I got lost', reflexive = haben).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: verlaufen
Wiktionary: verlaufen (German)

verlieren.etymology: From Middle High German verliesen (with Early New High German levelling of grammatical alternation s ~ r in favor of r) and Old High German firliosan ('to lose, forfeit, destroy'), from Proto-Germanic *fraleusaną (cognate with Old English forlēosan, English 'forlorn'), from PIE *lews- ('to loosen, sever').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): verlieren
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): verlieren

vermieten.etymology: From Middle High German vermieten and Old High German firmieten ('to hire out, let for rent'), formed with prefix ver- and mieten ('to hire, rent', OHG mietan, from Miete 'reward, pay, rent', OHG mieta).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): vermieten
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vermieten

vermögen.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge explain Vermögen (MHG vermügen) as the nominalized infinitive of vermögen ('to have power or means'), shifting from 'capability, power' to 'financial assets, fortune'.

morphemes.meaning: older sense 'to have power, be able' (compare Macht)

history.meaning: to be able, possess power or means (from mügen 'can, have power')
nominalized infinitive: capability -> financial means, fortune

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Vermögen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Vermögen

vermögen.notes: Shows the original meaning of mögen ('to have power', before it softened to 'to like'): das Vermögen means 'a fortune' (Das kostet ein Vermögen!) as well as 'capacity' in compounds like Erinnerungsvermögen.

verraten.etymology: Inseparable verb formed from the prefix 'ver-' (expressing change, loss, or wrongly doing something) and 'raten' (to guess, advise). 'Raten' comes from Old High German 'rātan' (to advise). Originally meaning to give bad advice, the term shifted toward meaning to betray someone or to reveal a secret.

cognates.meaning: to interpret symbols (from the same root for counsel/guess)

verraten.notes: It carries two distinct tones: the serious 'to betray (treason)' and the lighter 'to reveal (a secret or surprise)'.

verschieben.etymology: Middle High German verschieben ('to push aside, shift in space or time'), prefix derivative of schieben.

history.meaning: to shove out of place, push aside
to move furniture/objects; to postpone an appointment

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): verschieben
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): verschieben

verschieben.notes: Indispensable scheduling verb: Wollen wir den Termin auf Freitag verschieben? ('Shall we move/postpone the appointment to Friday?' — strong: verschob, hat verschoben).

verschließen.etymology: Continues Middle High German versliezen and Old High German firsliozan ('to lock up, shut fast'), formed from inseparable prefix ver- ('completely, shut away') and strong verb schließen ('to close, lock', OHG sliozan < Proto-Germanic *sleutaną).

history.meaning: to lock up, seal; (of a person) reserved

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Middle Low German/Dutch slot ('bolt, bar' = German Schloss)

verschließen.notes: While schließen simply means 'to close' (die Tür schließen), verschließen means 'to lock or seal shut' (ein verschlossenes Zimmer = a locked room).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): verschließen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): verschließen

verschluss.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from verschließen ('to lock up, close, seal', MHG versliezen, OHG firsliozan), modeled on Schluss ('closing, lock, conclusion', MHG sluz, from schließen 'to close, lock').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Verschluss
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Verschluss

verschmieren.etymology: Continues Middle High German versmirn, versmirwen ('to smear over, grease, soil'), formed from the inseparable prefix ver- ('all over, messily') and schmieren ('to smear, grease'). The base verb descends from Old High German smirwen and Proto-Germanic *smirwijaną ('to anoint, rub with grease'), a derivative of *smerwą ('fat, grease', preserved in German Schmer). Its everyday modern sense centres on wet ink, charcoal, or grease smudging across paper or glass.

cognates.meaning: close structural cousin; base smear < OE smerian

verschmieren.notes: German schmieren isn't always messy: ein Brot schmieren is the completely normal, everyday phrase for buttering or spreading a slice of bread.

verschnaufen.etymology: From Late Middle High German versnūfen ('to catch one's breath, recover breath after exertion'), formed with prefix ver- and schnaufen ('to breathe heavily, pant, snort', MHG snūfen).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): verschnaufen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): verschnaufen

verschwinden.etymology: Inherited from Middle High German verswinden and Old High German firswintan ('to vanish, waste away, faint'), combining inseparable ver- ('away, completely') with the strong verb schwinden ('to dwindle, shrink, fade'). Schwinden goes back to Old High German swintan and Proto-Germanic *swindaną ('to waste away, vanish'). While simplex schwinden today suggests gradual dwindling (as with strength or daylight), verschwinden expresses complete disappearance from view.
verschwinden.notes: English swindle was actually borrowed in the 18th century from German Schwindler, a cousin from the same root (originally someone 'dizzy' or making extravagant schemes vanish into thin air).

Wiktionary: verschwinden (German)

verschütten.etymology: From Middle High German verschüten ('to pour out accidentally, spill; to bury under rubble/earth'), formed with prefix ver- ('away, amiss, over') and schütten ('to pour, heap, shake', MHG schüten, OHG scutten).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): verschütten

versehen.etymology: Nominalized infinitive of reflexive sich versehen ('to look amiss, make an oversight, err', MHG sich versehen, OHG sih firsehan), formed from ver- ('amiss, wrongly') and sehen ('to see, look'), denoting an inadvertent mistake or oversight.

versprechen.etymology: From Middle High German versprechen and Old High German firsprehhan (originally 'to speak against, refuse, renounce; defend, pledge for', and from Late MHG 'to promise, pledge; reflexively: to misspeak'), formed from ver- and sprechen ('to speak').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): versprechen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): versprechen

verstecken.etymology: From Middle High German verstecken and Old High German firstecchen ('to stick away out of sight, conceal, hide'), formed with prefix ver- ('away, out of sight') and stecken ('to stick, put').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): verstecken
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): verstecken

verstehen.etymology: Continues Middle High German verstān, verstēn and Old High German firstān, farstantan ('to perceive, grasp, comprehend'), originally a West Germanic legal expression meaning 'to stand right before/around a case in court in order to represent or grasp it thoroughly', combining inseparable ver- (< OHG fir-/far- 'before, thoroughly') and stehen ('to stand').

history.meaning: to stand before/over a matter -> comprehend

cognates.meaning: Old English forstandan was the exact match of verstehen before understandan ('stand among/between') prevailed

verstehen.notes: Just like English understand and Ancient Greek epístamai ('I know how / understand', literally 'stand upon'), German conceptualized comprehension as taking a firm stance right in front of an issue.

versuchen.etymology: Inseparable verb combining 'ver-' and 'suchen' (to seek, search). 'Suchen' is from Old High German 'suohhen' and Proto-Germanic '*sōkijaną'. Initially, 'versuchen' meant to investigate thoroughly or to tempt. Over time, the primary meaning settled on 'to try' or 'to attempt', though the sense of 'to tempt' remains in specific contexts.
versuchen.notes: While it usually means 'to try', 'versuchen' can also mean 'to taste' (food) or 'to tempt' (someone).

vertauschen.etymology: From Late Middle High German vertūschen ('to exchange, swap, mix up by mistake'), formed with prefix ver- and tauschen ('to exchange, barter', Late MHG tūschen).

vertreterin.etymology: Feminine agent noun in -in from Vertreter ('representative, deputy'), derived from vertreten ('to step in place of someone, represent', MHG vertreten, from ver- + treten 'to step, tread').

morphemes.meaning: in place of, on behalf of

cognates.meaning: Old English tredan is the exact cognate of German treten

vertreterin.notes: Funny double meaning of vertreten: 'die Stadt vertreten' means 'to represent the city', whereas 'sich den Fuß vertreten' ('step wrong') means 'to twist one's ankle'!

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vertreten

verwechslung.etymology: Action/result noun formed with suffix -ung from verwechseln ('to exchange by mistake, confuse one thing with another', MHG verwehseln), from ver- ('amiss') + wechseln ('to change, exchange', OHG wehsalōn).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Verwechslung
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Verwechslung

verzeihen.etymology: From Old High German 'farzīhan' (to deny, renounce), which is composed of the prefix 'ver-' and the root of 'zeihen' (to accuse). The root traces back to Proto-Germanic '*tīhaną' (to declare, point out). The semantic progression moved from 'to renounce a claim' to 'to pardon or forgive a transgression'.

cognates.meaning: to instruct (from the same root meaning 'to point out')

verzeihen.notes: Used frequently in the polite apology 'Verzeihung!' (Forgive me! / Excuse me!).

viel.etymology: From Middle High German vil, vile and Old High German filu ('much, a great deal'), originally an indeclinable neuter u-stem substantive governing a partitive genitive, from Proto-Germanic *felu ('much', cognate with Old English fela), from PIE *pélh₁u ('much, many', cf. Greek polýs).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): viel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): viel

vielleicht.etymology: From Middle High German villīhte ('very easily, perhaps, maybe'), a univerbation of the intensifying adverb vil ('very, much', OHG filu) and līhte ('easily, lightly', adverb of līht > leicht 'light, easy').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): vielleicht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vielleicht

vier.etymology: From Middle High German vier and Old High German fior ('four'), from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr (cognate with English 'four'), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres ('four', cf. Latin quattuor, Greek téssares).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): vier
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vier

vierhändig.etymology: Compound derivational adjective formed from vier ('four', Old High German feor < Proto-Germanic *fedwōr), Hand ('hand', Old High German hant < Proto-Germanic *handuz), and the adjectival suffix -ig (Old High German -īg). As in einhändig and zweihändig, the suffix triggers regular i-umlaut of the root vowel from Hand to -händig. Although literally meaning 'having or using four hands', the word crystallized in 18th-century German musical culture for keyboard duets played by two performers seated at a single piano.

cognates.meaning: exact structural cognate of all parts

vierhändig.notes: The same pattern gives German einhändig ('one-handed'), zweihändig ('two-handed'), and beidhändig ('with both hands, ambidextrous').

Wiktionary: vierhändig (German)

vierte.etymology: Continues Old High German fiordo and Middle High German vierde ('fourth'), formed from the cardinal numeral vier ('four', OHG fior < Proto-Germanic *fedwōr) and the Indo-European ordinal suffix *-to- (Germanic *-þô > -te).
vierte.notes: After the irregular trio erste ('1st'), zweite (regular), and dritte ('3rd'), German ordinals from 4 to 19 simply add -te to the cardinal number: vierte, fünfte, sechste!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): vier
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vier

viertel.etymology: From Middle High German viertel, vierteil ('fourth part, quarter'), reduced compound of vier ('four', OHG fior) and Teil ('part, share', OHG teil, MHG teil).

vierteldrehung.etymology: Compound of Viertel ('quarter, fourth part', MHG viertel < vierteil 'fourth part') and Drehung ('turn, rotation', action noun in -ung from drehen 'to turn', OHG drāen).

cognates.meaning: Viertel = vier ('four') + Teil ('deal/part'); drehen ('to turn, twist') is cognate with Old English þrāwan ('twist -> throw')!

vierteldrehung.notes: Whether Werner is tuning the middle-D piano pin or Miriam is coaching Moritz on bread dough, eine Vierteldrehung ('a quarter turn') is the mark of precise craft!

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Viertel

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vierundvierzig

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vierzehn

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Vogel

von.etymology: From Old High German fona / fon and Middle High German von(e), marking origin, agency, or possession in place of the genitive; contracts with dem to vom.

sources.title: DWDS: von

von dem.etymology: Combination of the dative-governing preposition von ('from, of', MHG von, OHG fona, an expanded Old High German compound of *fana + *ana, related to Old Saxon fan) and dem ('the', masculine/neuter dative singular of der/das, OHG demu); routinely contracted since Middle High German (von deme > vome > vom) whenever dem is an unstressed definite article.

morphemes.meaning: the, that (masc./neut. dative sg. < OHG demu)

cognates.meaning: from the, of the (Dutch van matches German von)

von dem.notes: Grammar distinction: unstressed article von dem contracts to vom (vom Strand 'from the beach'), whereas demonstrative or relative dem stays uncontracted (von dem Mann da 'from that man'; der Film, von dem du sprichst).

vor.etymology: From Middle High German vor, vore and Old High German fora ('before, in front of'), from Proto-Germanic *furai ('in front, before', cognate with English 'before'), from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥h₂éy (locative of *per- 'forward, in front of', cf. Greek pará, Latin prae).

vorbeigucken.etymology: Colloquial separable prefix verb combining vorbei- ('past, by', univerbation of vor 'before, in front of' + bei 'by, near') and gucken ('to look, peek', MHG gucken, expressive Central/Northern German verb originally imitating a bird or child peeking out).

history.meaning: to look past something; colloquially: to drop in briefly

rootFamily.gloss: to look (often pronounced kucken in Northern Germany)
to stop by, drop in (more southern/standard synonym)

vorbeigucken.notes: In Northern Germany (including Hamburg), initial g- in gucken is habitually pronounced [k] (vorbeikucken), and 'dropping by for a quick look' means paying a brief visit.

vorbeikommen.etymology: Separable compound verb from vorbei ('past, by, over', from MLG vorbī) and kommen ('to come', OHG queman, MHG komen), meaning 'to come by, drop by, pass by'.

vorbeiströmen.etymology: Separable compound verb from vorbei ('past, by') and strömen ('to stream, flow', MHG ströumen, from Strom 'stream, current'), meaning 'to stream or flow past'.

vorbereiten.etymology: Separable prefix verb formed in Early New High German from temporal vor- ('beforehand, in advance', OHG fora) and bereiten ('to make ready, prepare', MHG bereiten, derived from bereit 'ready').

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vorbereiten

vorbereitung.etymology: Action noun in -ung derived from vorbereiten ('to prepare in advance'), combining vor- ('beforehand, in advance') with bereiten ('to make ready', MHG bereiten, from bereit 'ready').

history.meaning: to prepare ahead of time -> preparation

cognates.meaning: bereit shares its root *raidaz ('ready for the road') with English 'ready'!

vorbereitung.notes: Useful kitchen distinction: vorbereiten / Vorbereitung is 'prep work ahead of time' (chopping carrots), whereas zubereiten is 'cooking/making the dish itself'!

vorderwand.etymology: Architectural compound of vorder- ('front, anterior', MHG vorder, OHG fordaro, comparative formation to vor/fort) and Wand ('interior/partition wall', OHG and MHG want), denoting a front wall.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Vorderwand
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Vorderwand

vorfahren.etymology: Derived from the prefix 'vor-' (before, forward) and 'fahren' (to drive, travel). The underlying Germanic root *faranan broadly denotes movement or journeying. In modern German, the compound implies driving up to the front of a building or moving ahead. It has been used since Old High German.

history.meaning: to pull up, to drive up

vorfahren.notes: Think of it as 'faring forward' to the front door.

sources.title: DWDS

vorheizen.etymology: Formed from 'vor-' (before, in advance) and 'heizen' (to heat). The base verb traces back to the Proto-Germanic root *haitijanan, related to heat and fire. The prefix narrows the meaning to heating something prior to its use. The term became especially common with modern cooking and heating technology.
vorheizen.notes: Often used in recipes for preheating the oven.

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

vorhin.etymology: From Middle High German vorhin ('ahead, formerly, a little while ago'), compound adverb of vor ('before') and directional hin ('hence, away'); narrowed in New High German to the temporal sense 'a short while ago, earlier today'.

vorkoster.etymology: Agent noun formed with -er from vorkosten ('to taste food or drink beforehand', from vor- 'beforehand' + kosten 'to taste, sample', OHG kostōn, MHG kosten, from Proto-Germanic *kustōną 'to test, try, taste'), denoting an official food taster.

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Vorkoster

vorlesen.etymology: Separable prefix verb from Middle High German vorlesen ('to read aloud in front of someone'), combining spatial/demonstrative vor- ('before, in front of', OHG fora) and lesen ('to gather, read', OHG lesan, MHG lesen), calquing Latin praelegere.

history.meaning: to read aloud to students, lecture

vormittag.etymology: Early New High German temporal compound formed by hypostasis from the prepositional phrase vor Mittag ('before midday/noon'), combining vor ('before', OHG fora) and Mittag ('midday, noon', OHG mittitag, MHG mittetac).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Vormittag
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Vormittag

vorn.etymology: From Middle High German vorne, vornān and Old High German forna ('in front, ahead'), spatial adverb formed with locative suffixes from the Indo-European root *per-/*pr̥- (compare vor).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): vorn
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vorn

vornehm.etymology: Originates from the prefix 'vor-' and the verb 'nehmen' (to take). Historically, the adjective described someone who was 'taken out' or selected for their superior rank. Over time, it evolved to mean distinguished, elegant, or refined. The semantic shift from 'selected' to 'posh' occurred in Early Modern German.
vornehm.notes: Historically referred to people of high birth, but now means generally elegant or posh.

sources.title: DWDS

vorsagen.etymology: Separable prefix verb from Middle High German vorsagen and Old High German forasagēn ('to say beforehand, recite for someone to repeat, prompt, whisper an answer'), combining vor- ('before, in front of') and sagen ('to say', OHG sagēn).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): vorsagen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vorsagen

vorsicht.etymology: From Middle High German vorsiht and Old High German forasiht ('foresight, providence, caution, care'), verbal abstract noun to vorsehen ('to foresee, take precautions', OHG forasehan), calquing Latin prōvidentia.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Vorsicht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Vorsicht

vorsichtig.etymology: From Middle High German vorsihtic ('far-sighted, prudent, cautious, careful'), derived with suffix -ig from Vorsicht ('foresight, caution', MHG vorsiht).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): vorsichtig
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): vorsichtig

vorstellen.etymology: Constructed from 'vor-' (before) and 'stellen' (to place, set). The reflexive usage (sich etwas vorstellen) conceptually implies placing an image or idea before one's own mind. The root *stallijanan denotes positioning or setting up. The meaning 'to introduce' comes from placing a person before someone else.
vorstellen.notes: Use with reflexive dative (mir) for 'imagine', and accusative for 'introduce someone'.

völlig.etymology: From Middle High German völlic, vollic and Old High German follīh ('full, complete, abundant, entire'), derived from voll ('full', OHG fol) with suffix -ig/-lich.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): völlig
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): völlig

wach.etymology: Entered High German in the 16th century from Middle Low German wak, wake ('awake, alert'), replacing older MHG wacker in the sense 'awake', from the Proto-Germanic root *wak- ('to be awake, brisk', cf. wachen 'to wake, watch', OHG wahhēn, from PIE *weg- 'to be lively, strong').

wachen.etymology: Old High German wahhēn and Middle High German wachen ('to stay awake, keep watch'), sharing its Germanic root with die Wache ('guard, watch') and English 'wake / watch'.

wachs.etymology: Wachs continues Old High German and Middle High German wahs 'beeswax, wax' (8th/9th century), from Proto-Germanic *wahsą, the exact cognate of English wax (Old English weax), Dutch was, and Old Norse vax. Outside Germanic it matches Lithuanian vaškas and Old Church Slavonic voskŭ 'wax'; many Indo-Europeanists connect these forms further with a verbal root *wek- or *weg- 'to weave', referring to the woven cellular structure of the honeycomb. Historically, das Wachs ('wax') is unrelated to the strong verb wachsen ('to grow', English wax in 'wax and wane', from Proto-Germanic *wahsijaną), even though the two converged in sound.

rootFamily.gloss: to wax, treat with wax (weak verb: wachste)

wachs.notes: Two verbs spelled wachsen! Strong wachsen (er wächst, wuchs, ist gewachsen) means 'to grow', while weak wachsen (er wachst, wachste, hat gewachst — e.g. skis) means 'to coat with wax'.

wachsen.etymology: Old High German wahsan, Middle High German wahsen ('to grow, increase'), from Proto-Germanic *wahsijaną, cognate with English wax (of the moon).

cognates.meaning: to grow larger (as in 'the moon waxes and wanes')

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): wachsen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): wachsen

wachsen.notes: Strong change-of-state verb taking sein (wächst, wuchs, ist gewachsen); don't confuse it with weak wachsen ('to wax skis or wood', hat gewachst, from das Wachs)!

wachssiegel.etymology: A determinative compound of Wachs 'wax' and Siegel 'seal', naming an impression stamped with a signet ring or metal matrix into softened wax to authenticate documents or fasten letters against tampering. Wachs continues Old High German and Middle High German wahs 'beeswax', from Proto-Germanic *wahsą. Siegel continues Middle High German sigel (beside older Old High German insigili, Middle High German insigel), borrowed early from Latin sigillum 'small figure, statuette, seal impression', a diminutive of signum 'sign, mark'. Under the post-1996 spelling rule for compounds, both the s of Wachs and the initial s of Siegel are preserved (Wachssiegel).
wachssiegel.notes: Look closely at the double s in Wachssiegel: the first s belongs to Wachs [vaks] and the second starts Siegel [ˈziːɡəl], so you pronounce [ks] followed by [z] across the compound boundary.

wachstuch.etymology: A compound of Wachs 'wax' and Tuch 'cloth', attested since Early New High German (16th and 17th centuries), originally denoting coarse linen rubbed or coated with beeswax to wrap bales and protect travellers' gear from rain, and later applied to oil-varnished or plastic-coated wipeable fabric ('oilcloth', especially for kitchen tables). Wachs continues Old High German and Middle High German wahs 'beeswax', from Proto-Germanic *wahsą. Tuch continues Old High German tuoh and Middle High German tuoch 'cloth, kerchief', from Proto-Germanic *dōkaz (with the High German consonant shift turning d into t and final k into ch), cognate with Dutch doek 'cloth, canvas'.

cognates.meaning: heavy linen or cotton canvas (borrowed from Dutch doek)

wachstuch.notes: Even though modern wipeable tablecloths are coated with PVC or acrylic rather than beeswax, German still calls them Wachstuch ('wax-cloth') after their 16th-century ancestor.

iterative verb in -eln 'to totter, wobble, wiggle'

wahl.etymology: From Middle High German wal, wale and Old High German wala ('choice, selection, option, election'), from Proto-Germanic *walō ('choice', cognate with Old Norse val), derived from the PIE root *welh₁- ('to wish, will, choose', cf. wollen, Latin velle).

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Wahl

wahr.etymology: Wahr continues Old High German and Middle High German wār 'true', from Proto-Germanic *wēraz. It goes back to Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ros 'true', which also gave Latin verus and Old Irish fír. English lost the native adjective, but has the same root through French: very comes from Old French verai, from Latin verus. The phrase wahr machen ('to make true, carry out') and the compound wahrscheinlich ('probable', literally 'appearing true', 17th century) are built on this adjective.
wahr.notes: Don't mix it up with wahren/bewahren (to preserve) or wahrnehmen (to perceive): those come from a different root meaning 'to watch, guard', related to English beware.

wahrheit.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German wārheit ('truth, veracity, reality'), abstract noun formed with suffix -heit from wahr ('true', OHG wār, from Proto-Germanic *wēraz, cognate with Latin vērus 'true').

wald.etymology: From Middle High German walt, Old High German wald ('forest, wooded highland'), from Proto-Germanic *walþuz (cognate with English wold).

cognates.meaning: originally 'forest', later cleared 'rolling hills' (Cotswolds, The Weald)!

wand.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German want ('wall, partition wall'), originally denoting a woven wattle-and-daub wall, derived by ablaut from the strong verb winden ('to wind, plait, weave wickerwork', OHG wintan, Proto-Germanic *windaną). wanderer.etymology: Derived from the verb 'wandern' (to hike, wander) with the agent suffix '-er'. The core root *wandōjanan reflects a winding or roving movement. The noun designates someone who travels on foot, particularly through nature. It became culturally significant during the Romantic period.
wanderer.notes: A very common word in Germany, where hiking is a national pastime.

wandern.etymology: Traces back to the Proto-Germanic root *wandōjanan, meaning to turn or wind. The verb originally described an aimless or winding journey. In modern usage, it specifically refers to hiking or taking long walks. It is historically related to 'winden' (to wind or twist).

cognates.meaning: to move about without a fixed course

wandern.notes: Takes 'sein' as an auxiliary verb, as it denotes a change of location.

wandpaneel.etymology: Compound of Wand ('interior wall', OHG want, originally 'woven wattle wall', derived from winden 'to wind, plait') and Paneel ('wooden wall panel', borrowed via Middle Low German and Dutch paneel from Old French panel < Vulgar Latin *pannellum 'small rectangular piece of cloth or wood', diminutive of Latin pannus).

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Wandschalter

wann.etymology: From Middle High German wanne, wenne and Old High German hwanne, wanne ('when, at what time'), from Proto-Germanic *hwannē (cognate with English 'when'), built on the interrogative stem *hwa- (< PIE *kʷo-). Differentiated in New High German from conditional wenn.

warnschild.etymology: A transparent modern compound of the verb warnen 'to warn' and das Schild 'sign'. Warnen goes back to Old High German warnōn, Middle High German warnen 'to prepare, to take precautions, to warn', from Proto-Germanic *warnōną, the source also of English warn (Old English warnian). Schild continues Old High German scilt, Middle High German schilt 'shield', from Proto-Germanic *skelduz. Shields bearing coats of arms were hung up as identifying signs, and from this the meaning 'signboard' developed; in modern German the two senses split by gender (der Schild 'shield', das Schild 'sign').

history.meaning: to warn / shield, coat of arms

warnschild.notes: Gender trick: das Schild is the sign on the wall, der Schild is the knight's shield, so it is always das Warnschild.

wasserbecken.etymology: Determinative compound combining Wasser ('water', Old High German wazzar < Proto-Germanic *watōr) and Becken ('basin, bowl', Middle High German becken, Old High German beckīn). Becken was borrowed early into West Germanic from Vulgar Latin *baccīnum ('water vessel, bowl'), the same Gallo-Roman source that gave Old French bacin and English basin. In German courtyards and town squares, ein Wasserbecken typically denotes the carved stone catch-basin beneath a fountain spout.

wasserdicht.etymology: A compound of 'Wasser' (water) and 'dicht' (tight, dense). The adjective 'dicht' stems from the Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz, denoting something thick or solid. The combination describes a material impervious to water. It is also used metaphorically for arguments with no loopholes.
wasserdicht.notes: Used for both waterproof jackets and foolproof alibis.

wasserfarbe.etymology: A compound of Wasser 'water' and Farbe 'colour, paint', i.e. paint that is mixed with water. Wasser continues Old High German wazzar, from Proto-Germanic *watōr and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European r/n-stem *wódr̥ 'water'; the High German consonant shift turned the t into the ss heard today, while English water kept it. Farbe comes from Old High German farawa, Middle High German varwe, a noun built on the Germanic adjective *farwa- 'coloured'. The compound is the native counterpart of the loanword Aquarell, from Italian acquarello.
wasserfarbe.notes: Wasser vs water is a textbook example of the High German consonant shift: German ss/z where English has t (Wasser/water, Fuß/foot, Zunge/tongue).

wasserfest.etymology: Modern German compound adjective uniting Wasser ('water', Old High German wazzar < Proto-Germanic *watōr) with fest ('firm, fast, resistant', Middle High German veste, Old High German festi < Proto-Germanic *fastuz). Across technical and everyday German compounds—such as feuerfest, wetterfest, and wischfest—the adjective -fest developed into a productive second element meaning 'impervious or resistant to'. That usage mirrors older English compounds in -fast like colourfast and weather-fast.
wasserfest.notes: Think of English colourfast ('dye that holds fast in water'): German -fest is the exact cognate of English fast in its original sense of 'firm, immovable'.

wegfahren.etymology: Wegfahren is a separable compound of the directional adverb weg 'away, off' and the strong verb fahren 'to travel, go, drive'. The prefix weg- (pronounced with a short vowel) arose in Middle High German enwec, wec from the accusative phrase in weg 'onto the road, away', based on der Weg 'way, road'. Fahren continues Old High German faran and Proto-Germanic *faraną 'to travel, journey', cognate with English fare.

morphemes.meaning: away, off (from in weg 'on one's way')

cognates.meaning: same two Germanic roots (compare away and farewell)

wegfahren.notes: English 'away' came from Old English on weg ('on one's way') in the exact same way that German weg- grew out of in weg.

wegfliegen.etymology: Separable verb attested since late Middle High German and Early New High German, combining weg- ('away') with the strong verb fliegen ('to fly'). Fliegen continues Middle High German vliegen and Old High German fliogan from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą ('to fly'). The prefix weg- arose by apheresis from Middle High German enwec and Old High German in weg ('onto one's way, away'), making wegfliegen the exact structural twin of English fly away (from Old English on weg 'away').

morphemes.meaning: away (< OHG in weg 'on the way')

history.meaning: to fly away, blow off in the wind

cognates.meaning: both parts cognate: fly (< OE flēogan) + away (< OE on weg)

wegfliegen.notes: Pronunciation tip: the noun der Weg ('path, way') has a long vowel [veːk], whereas the adverb/prefix weg- ('away') kept its older short vowel [vɛk]!

wehen.notes: Wait—why is der Wind called 'wind'? Because in Proto-Indo-European, *h₂wéh₁-nt-s ('wind') was literally the present participle of the verb preserved in German wehen ('to blow')!

cognates.meaning: exact morpheme-by-morpheme cognates (Old English wā dōn = 'do woe')!

wehtun.notes: You can also spot Weh ('ache') in cosy German compounds like Heimweh ('homesickness'), Fernweh ('wanderlust, ache for faraway places'), and Kopfweh ('headache')!

wenigstens.etymology: Formed in Early New High German (16th to 17th century) from the superlative stem wenigst- of wenig ('little, few') plus the compound adverbial suffix -ens (originally a combination of weak declensional -en and adverbial genitive -s, as in mindestens and höchstens). Surprisingly, wenig itself descends from Middle High German wēnec and Old High German wēnag ('wretched, lamentable, pitifully small'), derived from the interjection wē ('woe!' < Proto-Germanic *wai). Over the Middle Ages, 'pitiful' bleached into the neutral quantifier 'small, little', from whose superlative wenigstens ('at the very least') emerged.

cognates.meaning: cognate with the underlying exclamation *wai (> OHG wē)

wenigstens.notes: Like bestens, höchstens, and mindestens, the ending -stens turns a superlative adjective directly into a sentence adverb.

wiedererkennen.etymology: Formed by combining 'wieder' (again) with 'erkennen' (to recognize). The base verb 'kennen' originates from the root *kannjanan, meaning to know or make known. The compound specifically refers to identifying someone or something previously known. It combines the prefix of repetition with the verb of perception.
wiedererkennen.notes: Separable verb: 'ich erkenne ihn wieder' (I recognize him).

wiederhören.etymology: A nominalization of the phrase 'wieder hören' (to hear again). The verb 'hören' comes from the Proto-Germanic *hauzijanan. As a fixed expression ('auf Wiederhören'), it serves as the standard telephone sign-off, equivalent to 'goodbye'. It parallels 'auf Wiedersehen' but is specific to auditory encounters.
wiederhören.notes: Almost exclusively used in 'Auf Wiederhören' when ending a phone call.

cognates.meaning: exact structural and etymological counterpart (English how and German wie both trace back to *hwō / *hwē!)

rootFamily.gloss: anyway, in any case (built from so + wie + so!)

wieso.notes: In conversational German, Wieso? (and Wieso denn?) is often preferred over textbook Warum? when reacting with surprise or mild challenge ('How come? / Wait, why?').

windfest.etymology: Compound adjective formed from Wind ('wind', Middle High German and Old High German wint < Proto-Germanic *windaz) and -fest ('firm, resistant', Old High German festi < Proto-Germanic *fastuz). Proto-Germanic *windaz itself continues Indo-European *h₂weh₁ntos ('blowing'), an old participial noun built to the verb root *h₂weh₁- ('to blow', preserved in German wehen). Modelled alongside wetterfest and wasserfest, windfest describes outdoor fixtures, garments, or table settings anchored firmly enough to withstand gusts.

cognates.meaning: exact cognate of first element (< OE wind)
exact cognate of second element (< OE fæst 'firm')

windfest.notes: German still keeps both ancient cousins side by side: der Wind ('the wind') and its underlying Indo-European verb wehen ('to blow').

windstoß.etymology: Inherited from Middle High German wintstōz ('sudden gust of wind'), a determinative compound of Wind ('wind', Old High German wint < Proto-Germanic *windaz) and Stoß ('push, thrust, jolt, blast'). Stoß continues Old High German stōz, the strong verbal noun to stoßen ('to push, thrust, strike' < Proto-Germanic *stautaną, from Indo-European *(s)tewd- 'to beat, push'). Literally a 'wind-thrust', the compound contrasts a sharp, isolated surge of air with steady blowing wind.
windstoß.notes: Compare Dutch windstoot: where Dutch kept Germanic -t at the end of stoot, High German shifted post-vocalic *-t to -ß in Stoß.

windtest.etymology: Modern German compound combining native Wind ('wind', Old High German wint < Proto-Germanic *windaz) with Test ('test, trial'). German borrowed der Test from English in the late 19th and early 20th centuries (initially in experimental psychology and engineering before becoming everyday usage). English test itself goes back via Old French test to Latin testum ('earthenware vessel, assaying cupel'), in which alchemists and minters tested the purity of precious metals.

cognates.meaning: matching compound of cognate Wind and source word Test

windtest.notes: Because der Test is a relatively young loanword from English, it keeps its English-style -s plural even in the German dative plural: nach den Windtests.

winterregen.etymology: A transparent compound of Winter and Regen 'rain'. Winter goes back to Old High German wintar, from Proto-Germanic *wintruz; its deeper origin is uncertain, with a link to the Indo-European root for 'wet, water' (*wed-) the most often cited proposal. Regen continues Old High German regan, Middle High German regen, from Proto-Germanic *regnaz, which also gave Old English regn, modern English rain. Compounds of this type (Sommerregen, Frühlingsregen) are freely formed in German.
winterregen.notes: English rain and German Regen are the same word: Old English regn lost its g in pronunciation, which German kept.

witz.etymology: Originates from the Proto-Germanic root *witją, meaning knowledge, understanding, or wit. Historically, it referred to intelligence or cognitive sharpness. Over time, the meaning shifted toward humor, jokes, and amusing anecdotes. This semantic shift from 'knowledge' to 'joke' happened largely in the 18th and 19th centuries.
witz.notes: 'Einen Witz machen' means to make a joke.

witzig.etymology: Witzig is formed from the noun Witz with the adjective suffix -ig; Middle High German already had witzec, witzic 'clever, sensible, of sound mind'. Witz continues Old High German wizzī 'knowledge, understanding', Middle High German witze, from Proto-Germanic *witją, a derivative of the root of wissen 'to know'. From the 17th and 18th centuries, partly under the influence of French esprit, Witz shifted from 'intelligence' to 'quick wit, clever remark' and then to 'joke', and witzig followed from 'clever' to 'funny'.
witzig.notes: English wit kept the old meaning 'mind, intelligence' (to be at one's wits' end), while German Witz moved almost entirely to 'joke'.

Because Old High German wār lost its final -r except before vowels in Middle High German, vowel-initial prepositions retain wor- (woran, worauf), whereas consonant-initial mit yields womit. It is the exact historical counterpart of English wherewith.

wusch.etymology: Expressive onomatopoeic interjection established in colloquial and narrative New High German to imitate the rushing hiss of air or an object shooting swiftly past. It stands beside the colloquial motion verb wuschen ('to slip or dart past quickly') and older Middle High German wüschen, wischen ('to glide swiftly, whisk'). Across Germanic languages, the sequence of labial glide [v/w], high back vowel [ʊ], and palato-alveolar sibilant [ʃ] iconically mimics a sudden gust or swoosh of air.

morphemes.meaning: sound of a swift rush through the air

cognates.meaning: parallel onomatopoeic formation imitating rushing air

wusch.notes: Watch the vowel length on the page: wusch! ('whoosh!') has a short [ʊ], while er wusch ('he washed', from waschen) has a long [uː].

wünschen.notes: Note reflexive dative for wishing for a gift or outcome for oneself: Ich wünsche mir Ruhe ('I'm wishing for peace and quiet'), vs. Ich wünsche dir viel Glück! ('I wish you good luck!').

würde.etymology: From Middle High German wirde, würde (with vowel rounding after w-) and Old High German wirdī ('worth, honor, dignity, high rank'), deadjectival abstract noun in *-īn- derived from wert ('worth, worthy', OHG werd).

würfel.etymology: Continues Old High German wurfil and Middle High German würfel ('six-sided game die; cube'), an instrument noun in -el (with i-umlaut u > ü) from the zero-grade of werfen ('to throw, cast', OHG werfan); literally 'the little thing that is thrown (in a dice game)'!

history.meaning: die (pl. dice); geometric cube; diced food cube

cognates.meaning: exact culinary metaphor: both English ('dice') and German (Würfel / würfeln) name food cubes after six-sided game dice!

würfel.notes: Just as English says 'to dice carrots' after game dice, German calls every cube—from geometry to diced soup carrots (Karottenwürfel) and sugar cubes (Zuckerwürfel)—der Würfel!

wütend.etymology: From Middle High German wüetende and Old High German wuotenti ('raging, furious, mad'), lexicalized present participle of wüten ('to rage, rave', OHG wuoten, denominative verb from Wut 'rage, fury, madness', OHG wuot < Proto-Germanic *wōdaz 'possessed, furious, inspired').

zart.etymology: Inherited from Middle High German zart ('beloved, dear, fine, delicate, soft') and late Old High German zart ('delicate, pampered'), alongside the verb Old High German zartōn ('to caress, fondle, treat gently'). Originally characteristic of Upper and Central German courtly poetry in the sense 'cherished, dainty', it spread across all varieties of German for fine textures, pale hues, and tender food. Its pre-Old High German ancestry outside High German remains uncertain, though Low German and Scandinavian borrowed it early (compare Danish sart).
zart.notes: Chocolate lovers meet this word on every German supermarket shelf: Zartbitterschokolade ('delicately bitter dark chocolate').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: zart
Wiktionary: zart (German)

zauberhaft.etymology: Derived in 18th-century German from Zauber ('magic, spell, enchantment') and the productive adjectival suffix -haft ('endowed with, having the nature of', from Old High German haft 'seized, possessing' < Proto-Germanic *haftaz). Zauber continues Middle High German zouber and Old High German zoubar from Proto-Germanic *taubrą ('sorcery, magic charm'), strikingly cognate with Old English tēafor ('red pigment, salve', reflecting the ancient Germanic practice of reddening carved runes). From 'produced by magic', zauberhaft softened in Romantic and modern German into 'enchanting, delightful'.
zauberhaft.notes: Mozart's Die Zauberflöte ('The Magic Flute', 1791) shares the exact same first element Zauber.

zedernkiste.etymology: Compound of Zeder ('cedar', OHG zēdarboum from Latin cedrus / Greek kédros) + Kiste ('box, chest', OHG kista from Latin cista); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Zeder and Kiste.

history.meaning: two early monastery/trade borrowings into Old High German

cognates.meaning: both elements go back to the same Greek/Latin cedrus + cista!

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Kiste

zedernkiste.notes: English chest and German Kiste are sibling early West Germanic loans from Latin cista (with Old English palatalizing c- -> ch-, while High German kept hard k-)!

zedernstab.etymology: Determinative compound combining Zeder ('cedar', joined with the weak inflectional linking element -n-) and Stab ('rod, staff, dowel', Old High German stab < Proto-Germanic *stabaz). Zeder descends from Middle High German zēder and Old High German zēdarboum, borrowed via Latin cedrus from Ancient Greek kédros ('cedar, fragrant juniper'). Because Medieval Latin pronounced c before e as [ts], German spelled the borrowed tree name with initial Z-.

cognates.meaning: from the same Latin cedrus via Old French cèdre

zedernstab.notes: Latin words beginning with ce- or ci- regularly start with Z- [ts] in German: cedrus → Zeder, cella → Zelle (cellar/cell), circulus → Zirkel.

zehe.etymology: From Middle High German zēhe, Old High German zēha ('toe'), from Proto-Germanic *taihwōn- (cognate with English toe).

cognates.meaning: digit of the foot (< Old English tā)

rootFamily.gloss: to point, show (from the same PIE root!)

zehn.etymology: From Middle High German zehen, zēn and Old High German zehan ('ten'), from Proto-Germanic *tehun (cognate with English 'ten', Gothic taihun), from Proto-Indo-European *dékm̥ ('ten', cf. Latin decem, Greek déka).

cognates.meaning: ordinal of ten (and archaic tithe < Old English tēogoþa)

zeichen.etymology: Traces back to the Proto-Germanic noun *taikną, denoting a sign, token, or mark. It is related to the verb *teikijanan (to show). The word encompasses physical signals, symbols, and meaningful gestures. It has been a central term for semiotics in the German language since the medieval period.
zeichen.notes: Used for everything from a traffic sign to a secret signal.

zeichnung.etymology: From Middle High German zeichenunge and Old High German zeihhanunga ('marking, designation, sign; from Early New High German also drawing, sketch'), action/result noun in -ung from zeichnen ('to mark, draw', OHG zeihhanen, from Zeichen 'sign, token').

Latin dīcere, Greek deíknȳmi).

zeitkapsel.notes: Latin capsa ('box') gave German both die Kasse ('cash register') and its diminutive die Kapsel ('capsule').

ziemlich.etymology: Continues Middle High German zimelich ('proper, fitting, seemly, moderate') and Old High German zimilīh ('fitting, appropriate'). It derives from the old strong verb Middle High German zemen, Old High German zeman ('to be fitting, suit, beseem', surviving in formal German ziemen), from Proto-Germanic *temaną ('to fit together') and Indo-European *dem- ('to build, fit'). In the 16th and 17th centuries, 'to a proper, respectable extent' bleached into the everyday degree adverb 'fairly, quite, rather', exactly paralleling English fairly (from fair 'seemly') and Dutch tamelijk.

morphemes.meaning: to be fitting, suit (stem of ziemen)

history.meaning: to a fitting or considerable degree

cognates.meaning: fairly, rather (underwent the exact same semantic shift)
ablaut relative from the same root *tem- / *tam- (German zahm)

ziemlich.notes: Notice how unziemlich ('unseemly, improper') froze the old medieval meaning of 'fitting', while bare ziemlich marched on to mean 'pretty, rather'!

zimmermannsbleistift.etymology: Compound noun joining Zimmermann ('carpenter', linked with genitive -s-) and Bleistift ('pencil'). Zimmermann continues Middle High German zimberman and Old High German zimbarman, whose first element zimbar (< Proto-Germanic *timrą 'building wood', exact cognate of English timber) originally meant 'wooden construction' before narrowing to a single 'room' (das Zimmer). Bleistift arose in the 17th century from Blei ('lead', Old High German blīo, because newly discovered graphite was mistaken for lead ore) plus Stift ('stylus, peg'), here naming the flat rectangular pencil built not to roll off roof beams.

cognates.meaning: exact cognate of Zimmer in its original wooden-building sense (< OE timber)

zimmermannsbleistift.notes: Der Zimmermann preserves the ancient meaning of Zimmer ('timber'): a carpenter isn't a 'room-man', a room was originally a 'timbered space'!

zittern.etymology: From Middle High German zitern and Old High German zittarōn ('to tremble, shiver, shake, quake'), from Proto-Germanic *titurōną (cognate with Old Norse titra 'to shiver, twinkle'), a reduplicated intensive formation (*ti-tr-) to the PIE root *der- ('to burst, split, flay, jerk').
