Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zittern

zu.etymology: Recorded in Old High German in stressed form zuo and unstressed zi / za, and in Middle High German as zuo / ze. Modern zu serves as dative preposition ('to'), infinitive marker, degree adverb ('too'), and predicative/separable 'shut'.

sources.title: DWDS: zu
Wiktionary: zu (German)

zu.notes: Contracts with dem to zum and with der to zur.

zubinden.etymology: Zubinden continues Middle High German zuobinden and Old High German zuobintan, combining the separable particle zu- with the strong verb binden 'to tie, bind'. Here zu- carries its closing sense 'shut, closed', just as in zumachen 'to close'. Binden goes back through Old High German bintan and Proto-Germanic *bindaną to the Proto-Indo-European root *bhendh- 'to tie, bind' (compare Sanskrit bandh- and English bind and band).
zubinden.notes: In separable verbs, German zu- often means 'closed' (zubinden, zumachen, zuschließen), opposite to auf- ('open').

sources.title: DWDS: zubinden
DWDS / Pfeifer: binden
Wiktionary: zubinden (German)

zucker.etymology: From Middle High German zucker ('sugar'), borrowed in the 12th/13th century via Old Italian zucchero from Arabic sukkar (سُكَّر), which came via Persian shakar from Sanskrit śárkarā ('gravel, grit, crystallized sugar granules').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Zucker
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Zucker

zuckerglas.etymology: Compound of Zucker ('sugar', MHG zucker, borrowed via Italian zucchero from Arabic sukkar < Persian šakar < Sanskrit śarkarā 'gravel, candied sugar crystals') and Glas ('glass; glass jar', OHG glas < Proto-Germanic *glasą).

cognates.meaning: exact loanword and native cognate pair

zuckerglas.notes: In a German kitchen, das Glas covers both a drinking glass (Trinkglas) and a glass storage jar with a lid (Zuckerglas, Honigglas, Marmeladenglas)!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Zucker
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Zucker

zuckerguss.etymology: Culinary compound of Zucker ('sugar', MHG zucker) and Guss ('pouring, casting, poured coating', MHG and OHG guz, verbal noun to gießen 'to pour'), denoting sugar icing or glaze.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Zuckerguss
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Zuckerguss

zudrehen.etymology: Separable prefix verb combining directional/closing zu- ('closed, shut, toward', OHG zuo) and drehen ('to turn, twist', OHG drāen, MHG dræjen), meaning 'to turn off (a tap/valve) by twisting, screw shut, or turn toward'.

history.meaning: to turn off (a faucet), screw shut

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zudrehen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zudrehen

zuerst.etymology: From Middle High German ze ērst and Old High German zi ērist ('at first, first of all'), univerbation of the prepositional phrase zu ('to, at', OHG zi, zuo) + erst ('first', OHG ērist, superlative of ē 'before, early').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zuerst
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zuerst

zufall.etymology: From Middle High German zuoval ('that which falls to someone or happens unexpectedly, occurrence, accident, chance'), coined in 14th-century German mysticism as a loan translation of Latin accidēns ('what befalls, accidental property, chance event', from ad- + cadere 'to fall to').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Zufall
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Zufall

zufallen.etymology: Formed from 'zu-' (closed, towards) and 'fallen' (to fall). The verb 'fallen' stems from the Proto-Germanic *fallanan. In this context, it describes the action of a door or lid dropping or swinging shut naturally under its own weight. It can also refer to eyes closing from fatigue.
zufallen.notes: Takes 'sein' as an auxiliary verb, indicating a change of state.

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

zuflüstern.etymology: Constructed from the prefix 'zu-' (towards) and the verb 'flüstern' (to whisper). The base verb is of onomatopoeic origin, imitating the sound of hushed speech. The compound indicates directing a whisper specifically to another person. It has been standard in written German since the Early Modern period.
zuflüstern.notes: Always takes a dative object for the person being whispered to.

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

zufrieden.etymology: Derived from the phrase 'zu Frieden' (at peace). The noun 'Frieden' comes from the Proto-Germanic *friþuz, meaning peace or tranquility. The adjective describes a state of inner contentment and satisfaction with one's circumstances. The transition from a prepositional phrase to an adjective happened in Middle High German.

cognates.meaning: not under control (from the same root of love/peace)

zufrieden.notes: Often constructed with 'mit' (with) plus the dative case.

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

zug.etymology: Old High German zug and Middle High German zuc ('act of pulling, procession, draft'), a verbal noun from ziehen ('to pull'). With the arrival of railways in the 19th century, a string of pulled carriages became Eisenbahnzug and simply der Zug.

sources.title: DWDS: Zug
Wiktionary: Zug (German)

zugang.etymology: Continues Old High German zuogang and Middle High German zuoganc ('approach, access, entry'), combining directional prefix zu- ('toward, to') with Gang ('walk, way, passage', verbal noun of gehen).
zugang.notes: Notice the German -gang family built from gehen: Eingang ('entrance'), Ausgang ('exit'), Durchgang ('passageway'), Zugang ('access'), and Übergang ('transition')!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Zugang
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Zugang

zugfahrt.etymology: Compound of Zug ('pull, procession; since the 19th c. railway train, calquing English/French train', MHG zuc, OHG zug, verbal noun to ziehen 'to pull') and Fahrt ('journey, trip, drive', OHG and MHG vart, from fahren), denoting a train journey.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Zugfahrt
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Zugfahrt

zuhause.etymology: Nominalization of the locative prepositional phrase zu Hause ('at home', MHG ze hūse, OHG zi hūse, with preserved old dative singular ending -e on Haus 'house'), denoting one's home.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Zuhause
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Zuhause

zuhören.etymology: Separable prefix verb from Middle High German zuohœren and Old High German zuohōren ('to listen attentively to'), combining directional zu- ('toward, at') and hören ('to hear, listen', OHG hōren).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zuhören
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zuhören

zuklappen.etymology: Separable prefix verb combining closing zu- ('shut, closed') and klappen ('to clap, flap, fold with a snap', Late MHG klappen), meaning 'to fold shut, snap closed'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zuklappen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zuklappen

zuknöpfen.etymology: Formed by combining 'zu-' (closed) with 'knöpfen' (to button). The verb stems from 'Knopf' (button), rooted in the Proto-Germanic *knuppaz, denoting a knob or lump. The verb means to fasten clothing by pushing buttons through holes. It became common as buttons replaced laces in European clothing.
zuknöpfen.notes: Can also be used figuratively ('zugeknöpft sein') meaning to be reserved or uncommunicative.

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

zum.etymology: Standard contraction of the preposition zu ('to') with the masculine or neuter dative singular article dem (Middle High German zem / zum).

sources.title: DWDS: zum
Wiktionary: zum (German)

zumachen.etymology: Separable compound of stressed zu ('shut, closed') + machen ('make'), serving in everyday speech alongside schließen ('to close').

sources.title: DWDS: zumachen
Wiktionary: zumachen (German)

zunicken.etymology: A compound of 'zu-' (towards) and 'nicken' (to nod). The base verb is likely of expressive or frequentative origin, related to bowing the head. The compound specifically signifies directing a nod of acknowledgment or greeting toward someone. It appears frequently in literature to describe silent communication.
zunicken.notes: Takes a dative object indicating the person being nodded to.

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

zur.etymology: Standard contraction of the preposition zu ('to') with the feminine dative singular article der (Middle High German zer / zur).

sources.title: DWDS: zur
Wiktionary: zur (German)

zurück.etymology: From Middle High German zerucke, ze rucke and Old High German zi rucke ('behind one's back, backward, back'), univerbation of the prepositional phrase zu ('to, toward', OHG zi) + Rücken ('back', OHG rucki, MHG rucke).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zurück
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zurück

zurückbringen.etymology: Separable compound verb from zurück ('back', MHG zerucke) and bringen ('to bring, take', OHG bringan, MHG bringen), meaning 'to bring back, return'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zurückbringen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zurückbringen

zurückfedern.etymology: Compound separable verb from zurück- ('back') and federn ('to be elastic, bounce like a spring'), derived from Feder ('feather; metal spring', OHG fedara < Proto-Germanic *feþrō).

history.meaning: elastic metal strip or coil spring

cognates.meaning: German die Feder means both 'feather' and 'mechanical spring' (from the elasticity of a quill)!

zurückfedern.notes: Why does federn mean 'to bounce like a spring'? Because in German die Feder means a bird's feather, a writing quill, AND a bouncy metal spring!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): federn
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): federn

zurückkommen.etymology: Separable compound verb from zurück ('back', MHG zerucke) and kommen ('to come', OHG queman, MHG komen), meaning 'to come back, return'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zurückkommen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zurückkommen

zurücktreten.etymology: Separable compound verb from zurück ('back', MHG zerucke) and treten ('to step, tread', OHG tretan, MHG treten), meaning 'to step back, recede, resign from office'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zurücktreten
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zurücktreten

zurückziehen.etymology: Separable compound verb from zurück ('back', MHG zerucke) and ziehen ('to pull, draw, move', OHG ziohan, MHG ziehen), meaning 'to pull back, withdraw, retire'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zurückziehen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zurückziehen

zusagen.etymology: Combines 'zu-' (towards) and 'sagen' (to say). The root *sagjanan originally meant to speak or tell. The compound took on the meaning of giving one's word, confirming an appointment, or agreeing to a proposal. It can also mean that something appeals to someone.
zusagen.notes: As 'to appeal to', it takes the dative (e.g. 'Das sagt mir zu').

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

zusammen.etymology: From Middle High German zesamene, zesamen and Old High German zisamane ('together, into one place'), univerbation of the preposition zi ('to', > zu) and the adverbial derivative samane ('together', from samo 'same', Proto-Germanic *samana, cognate with Sanskrit samaná 'together').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zusammen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zusammen

zusammenbinden.etymology: Continues Middle High German zesamenebinden ('to tie or fasten together'), combining separable prefix zusammen- ('together', OHG zisamane) with strong verb binden ('to bind, tie', OHG bintan < Proto-Germanic *bindaną).

history.meaning: to tie together into a bundle

cognates.meaning: exact Germanic cognate with identical i–a–u ablaut (bind – bound = binden – band – gebunden)

zusammenbinden.notes: In French cooking a tied bundle of thyme and parsley is a 'bouquet garni'—in Miriam's kitchen it is simply 'zwei frische Zweige mit Schnur zusammengebunden'!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zusammenbinden
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zusammenbinden

zusammenbringen.etymology: Separable compound of zusammen ('together', OHG zisamane) + mixed verb bringen ('to bring', OHG bringan); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under zusammenbringen.

history.meaning: to gather, unite, bring people or parts together

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zusammenbringen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zusammenbringen

zusammenbringen.notes: Mixed conjugation like bringen: Musik bringt Menschen zusammen -> brachte zusammen -> hat zusammengebracht.

zusammenfalten.etymology: Separable compound verb from Middle High German zesamene valten ('to fold together'), combining zusammen ('together', OHG zisamane) and falten ('to fold', OHG faltan, MHG valten, Proto-Germanic *falþaną).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zusammenfalten
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zusammenfalten

zusammengeklappt.etymology: Past participle of zusammenklappen ('to fold up, fold together'), formed from zusammen ('together') and geklappt (past participle of klappen 'to fold, flap'), meaning 'folded up, collapsed'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zusammengeklappt
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zusammengeklappt

zusammenklappen.etymology: Separable compound verb combining zusammen ('together', OHG zisamane) and klappen ('to flap, fold', Late MHG klappen), meaning 'to fold up, fold together, collapse'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zusammenklappen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zusammenklappen

zusammenpassen.etymology: Zusammenpassen is a modern German separable compound of zusammen 'together' and passen 'to fit, suit'. Zusammen continues Old High German zisamane, formed from zi 'to' and saman 'together' (from Proto-Germanic *samana, related to English same). Passen entered German around 1500 via Middle Low German and Middle Dutch passen 'to be fitting, measure up', borrowed from Old French passer 'to pass, cross a mark'.

cognates.meaning: cognate roots of the two parts

zusammenpassen.notes: Hidden inside German zusammen is the exact relative of English 'same': things brought zusammen become 'one and the same' group.

sources.title: DWDS: zusammenpassen
DWDS / Pfeifer: passen
Wiktionary: zusammenpassen (German)

zusammenstehen.etymology: Separable compound verb from Middle High German zesamene stān ('to stand together, stand united'), combining zusammen ('together') and stehen ('to stand', OHG stēn, stān).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zusammenstehen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zusammenstehen

zuschauen.etymology: Separable prefix verb from Middle High German zuoschouwen and Old High German zuoscouwōn ('to look on, watch as a spectator'), combining directional zu- ('at, toward') and schauen ('to look, gaze', OHG scouwōn).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zuschauen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zuschauen

zuschneiden.etymology: Formed from 'zu-' (towards an end) and 'schneiden' (to cut). The verb comes from the Proto-Germanic *snīþanan. The compound typically means to cut material to a specific shape, size, or pattern, especially in tailoring. It reflects the meticulous preparation of materials before assembly.
zuschneiden.notes: Often used in the context of tailoring or adapting something specifically for someone.

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

zustehen.etymology: Separable prefix verb continuing Middle High German zuostān, zuostēn ('to step toward; to belong to, befittingly pertain to, be due to'), combining zu- ('to, toward', OHG zuo) and stehen ('to stand', OHG stān/stēn).

history.meaning: to stand by; to belong or be due to someone
to be rightfully owed or entitled to (with dative)

cognates.meaning: to allow, permit, grant (from the same prefix + verb combination)

zustehen.notes: Takes a dative beneficiary: Der Urlaub steht mir zu! ('I am entitled to that vacation!' — literally 'the vacation stands/belongs to me').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: zustehen
Wiktionary: zustehen (German)

zuständig.etymology: 16th-century Early New High German legal and administrative adjective formed with suffix -ig (and regular i-umlaut) from Zustand in its older sense of 'what rightfully pertains or belongs to someone' (verbal abstract of zustehen 'to pertain to, fall within one's purview').

morphemes.meaning: standing, jurisdiction (umlauted stem of Stand / stehen)

history.meaning: rightfully belonging to; having legal jurisdiction
in charge of, responsible for, competent

rootFamily.gloss: to be owed or entitled to

zuständig.notes: Construes with für + accusative: Ich bin hier für die Sicherheit zuständig ('I am in charge of security here') — marking institutional role rather than moral blame (verantwortlich).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: zuständig
Wiktionary: zuständig (German)

zutat.etymology: Zutat goes back to Middle High German zuotāt 'addition, something added', a compound of the particle zu 'to, in addition' and Tat 'deed, act'. The underlying idea is 'what is done or put in addition', parallel to the verb hinzutun 'to add'. Tat continues Old High German tāt, from Proto-Germanic *dēdiz, an abstract noun from the Indo-European root *dʰeh₁- 'to put, place, do', which also underlies tun and English do and deed. The narrowing to 'ingredient in cooking' is a later specialisation of the general sense 'addition, accessory'.
zutat.notes: Think of it as 'something you do in(to) the bowl': zu + tun gives Zutat, just as English deed comes from do.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: Zutat
Wiktionary: Zutat (German)

zuverlässig.etymology: 17th-century derivative built on the reflexive phrase sich zu jemandem / auf etwas verlassen ('to rely or depend upon someone/something', from verlassen in its MHG sense 'to entrust oneself to, rely on') with suffix -ig, meaning 'reliable, dependable, trustworthy'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zuverlässig
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zuverlässig

zuvor.etymology: A fusion of the preposition 'zu' and 'vor' (before). The components trace back to the Proto-Germanic roots *tō and *fura. The adverb is used to denote an event or state occurring previously or in advance of another. It has been a common temporal adverb since Middle High German.
zuvor.notes: Very common in the phrase 'wie nie zuvor' (like never before).

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

zuwinken.etymology: Constructed from 'zu-' (towards) and 'winken' (to wave). The verb stems from the Proto-Germanic *winkaną, meaning to move back and forth. The compound describes directing a gesture of greeting or farewell to someone with the hand. It is a standard term for waving at someone.

cognates.meaning: to close and open one eye quickly

zuwinken.notes: Requires a dative object indicating the person being waved at.

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

zwanzig.etymology: From Middle High German zweinzic and Old High German zweinzug ('twenty, two tens'), compound of the masculine dative/combining form zwein ('two', OHG zwēne) and the decade noun -zug ('group of ten', Proto-Germanic *twai tigiwiz, cognate with English 'twenty').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zwanzig
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zwanzig

zwei.etymology: From Middle High German and Old High German zwei (originally the neuter form beside masculine zwēne and feminine zwā, zwō, generalized to all genders by the 18th c.), from Proto-Germanic *twai (cognate with English 'two'), from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ ('two', cf. Latin duo, Greek dýo).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zwei
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zwei

zweig.etymology: Old High German zwīg, Middle High German zwīc ('branch, forking shoot'), built on the numeral root *twi- ('two, forked in two'), cognate with English twig.

history.meaning: forked shoot splitting in two, branch

cognates.meaning: small shoot (unshifted initial tw- vs. German zw-!)

rootFamily.gloss: to branch off (of a road or wire)

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Zweig
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Zweig

zweig.notes: Look at the initial zw- in zwei ('two'), Zweig ('branch that forks in two'), zwischen ('between two'), and Zweifel ('twofold mind = doubt') — all match English tw- (two, twig, betwixt)!

zweihundert.etymology: A compound numeral of zwei 'two' and hundert 'hundred'. Zwei continues Old High German zwei (originally the neuter form beside masculine zwēne and feminine zwā), from Proto-Germanic *twai and Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. Hundert comes from Old High German hunt 'hundred', later extended to hundert after the model of Old Saxon hunderod, with a second element related to Gothic rathjo 'number'. The base *hunda- reflects Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm 'hundred', the source also of Latin centum.
zweihundert.notes: Latin centum, English hundred and German hundert are the same Indo-European word; Grimm's law turned k into h in Germanic.

zweimal.etymology: From Middle High German zwei māl ('two times, twice', replacing the older inherited multiplicative adverb zwir, OHG zwiro 'twice'), combining zwei ('two') and Mal ('point in time, occasion').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zweimal
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zweimal

zweite.etymology: Formed in the 15th century with the ordinal suffix -te directly from the cardinal numeral zwei ('two'), gradually replacing the older suppletive ordinal ander ('other, second', OHG andar, MHG ander) to distinguish 'second' from 'other'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zweite
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zweite

zweitens.etymology: Early New High German enumerative adverb formed from the ordinal adjective zweite ('second') with the adverbial genitive ending -ens ('secondly, in the second place').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zweitens
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zweitens

zwiebel.etymology: Continues Old High German zwibollo and Middle High German zwibolle ('onion'), borrowed from Late Latin cēpulla ('small onion', diminutive of Latin cēpa 'onion', > Italian cipolla), folk-etymologically reshaped in Old High German as if built from zwi- ('two, double') + bollo ('bulb, ball')!

cognates.meaning: direct descendant of the same Late Latin cēpulla!
from the base Latin noun cēpa ('onion') via Old French

zwiebel.notes: Delightful folk etymology: when ancient German speakers borrowed Roman cēpulla ('onion'), they heard it as zwi-bollo—literally a 'double-layered bulb'!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Zwiebel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Zwiebel

zwillingskoffer.etymology: Compound of Zwilling ('twin', MHG zwillinc, OHG zwiniling, derived from zwei 'two', with genitival linking -s-) and Koffer ('suitcase, trunk', borrowed in the 16th/17th c. from French coffre < Latin cophinus 'basket, chest'), denoting a matching twin suitcase.

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Zwillingskoffer

zwischen.etymology: Grammaticalized by ellipsis of the preposition from the Middle High German phrase in zwischen, under zwischen and Old High German in zwiskēn, untar zwiskēn ('in the space of each of two, between'), where zwiskēn is the dative plural of the distributive adjective zwisk ('twofold, each of two', derived from zwei 'two', cognate with English 'betwixt').

history.meaning: in the middle of two, between

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zwischen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zwischen

zwölf.etymology: From Middle High German zwelf (with rounding of e > ö between w and l) and Old High German zwelif ('twelve'), from Proto-Germanic *twalif ('two left over [beyond ten]', cognate with English 'twelve', Gothic twalif), a compound of *twa- ('two') and *-lif- (from PIE *leykʷ- 'to leave over, remain', as in elf 'eleven').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zwölf
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zwölf

zwölft.etymology: Derived from the numeral 'zwölf' (twelve) with the ordinal suffix '-t'. 'Zwölf' originates from the Proto-Germanic compound *twaliwiz, meaning 'two left over' (after counting to ten). It signifies the position number twelve in a sequence. The formation of ordinals with a dental suffix is common across Germanic languages.
zwölft.notes: Declines like a regular adjective (e.g. der zwölfte Mann).

sources.title: DWDS

zählen.etymology: Continues Old High German zellen and Middle High German zeln ('to count, enumerate, recount'), derived with i-umlaut from Zahl ('number, tale', OHG zala < Proto-Germanic *talō 'calculation, number, narrative').

history.meaning: to count (with silent length-marking h after die Zahl)

cognates.meaning: Old English tellan ('to count, tell') and talu ('number, tale') are exact cognates!

zählen.notes: Notice how German split the two old senses of *taljaną cleanly: zählen means 'to count numbers', while erzählen means 'to tell a story' — just as English 'tell' still means 'count' in 'bank teller' and 'all told'!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zählen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zählen

ähnlich.etymology: Originates from the Old High German 'anagilīh', combining 'ana' (on, upon) and 'gilīh' (like, alike). The core root *galīkaz implies having the same body or form. The adjective denotes a resemblance or comparability between things. Over centuries, the prefix fused firmly with the root.
ähnlich.notes: Used with the dative case (e.g. 'er ist seinem Vater ähnlich').

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

ändern.etymology: Inherited from Middle High German endern, anderen and late Old High German andarōn ('to make other, alter, change'). It is a denominative verb formed from the adjective ander ('other, second', Old High German andar < Proto-Germanic *anþeraz < Indo-European *h₂énteros), with i-umlaut of a to ä triggered by Middle High German inflectional variants and analogy. Because it literally means 'to make different', ändern applies to modifying an existing plan, time, or text rather than swapping one separate object for another (wechseln).

cognates.meaning: to change (built on cognate stem anderen)
cognate with base ander (< OE ōþer, with regular loss of n before þ)

ändern.notes: English other and German ander look surprisingly different only because Old English regularly dropped n before th and lengthened the vowel (*anþer > ōþer > other)!

Wiktionary: ändern (German)

ärger.etymology: Back-formed in Early New High German from the verb ärgern ('to make worse, offend, annoy, anger', MHG ergern, OHG argirōn), which was built on ärger, the historical comparative of arg ('bad, wicked, base, severe', OHG arg, Proto-Germanic *argaz).

history.meaning: to make worse, corrupt, give offense

cognates.meaning: Old English earg ('cowardly, vile, wretched') is the exact cognate of German arg

ärger.notes: In everyday idioms Ärger bekommen / Ärger machen means 'to get into trouble / cause trouble'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer: Ärger
Wiktionary: Ärger (German)

ärmel.etymology: Old High German armilo, Middle High German ermel ('garment part covering the arm'), diminutive derivative of Arm ('arm').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Ärmel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Ärmel

ärmel.notes: Super intuitive: der Arm is your anatomical arm, and der Ärmel (zero plural: die Ärmel) is the shirt or coat sleeve around it — krempeln wir die Ärmel hoch! ('let's roll up our sleeves!').

äußere.etymology: From Middle High German ūzer, iuzer and Old High German ūzaro ('outer, external, exterior'), comparative adjective formed from the spatial adverb/preposition aus ('out', OHG ūz, Proto-Germanic *ūt, cognate with English 'outer' and 'utter').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): äußere
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): äußere

öffentlich.etymology: From Middle High German offenlīch (with secondary umlaut and excrescent dental -t- after -n- in Early New High German, parallel to eigentlich, ordentlich, wesentlich) and Old High German offanlīh ('open to all, public, manifest'), derived from offen ('open', OHG offan) + -lich.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): öffentlich
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): öffentlich

öffnen.etymology: Derived from the adjective offen ('open') via Old High German offanōn and Middle High German offenen / öffnen ('to make open').

sources.title: DWDS: öffnen
Wiktionary: öffnen (German)

öffnung.etymology: From Middle High German offenunge and Old High German offanunga ('opening, disclosure, aperture, gap'), action and result noun in -ung derived from öffnen ('to open', OHG offanōn, from offen 'open').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Öffnung
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Öffnung

öl.etymology: Old High German oli, Middle High German öle / öl, early borrowing from Vulgar Latin *ŏlium < Classical Latin ŏlĕum ('olive oil').

history.meaning: oil (whose following -i- triggered Germanic umlaut o > ö!)

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French oile from the same Vulgar Latin *olium

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Öl
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Öl

öl.notes: Covers cooking oil (Olivenöl), wood-finishing oil (Holzöl), hinge oil, and artist's oil paint (Ölfarbe); idiom: Öl ins Feuer gießen ('add fuel to the fire').

ölen.etymology: Continues Middle High German ölen ('to anoint or lubricate with oil'), derived from Öl ('oil', OHG oli, MHG öl < Vulgar Latin olium < Classical Latin oleum 'olive oil').

history.meaning: to rub or treat with oil

cognates.meaning: from the same Latin oleum via Old French oile

ölen.notes: In German, 'wie geölt laufen' ('to run as if oiled') is a lively everyday idiom for 'to run like clockwork'!

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): ölen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): ölen

üben.etymology: Continues Old High German uoben ('to till the soil, carry out, practice') and Middle High German üeben ('to put into action, cultivate, practise'), from Proto-Germanic *ōbijaną < PIE *h₃ep- ('to work, produce', cognate with Latin opus 'work'!).

cognates.meaning: from the same PIE root *h₃ep- ('to work, practice' — whence English 'opera', 'operate')!

üben.notes: Every music student in Germany knows the proverb 'Übung macht den Meister' ('Practice makes the master = Practice makes perfect')!

Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): üben

über.etymology: From Middle High German über and Old High German ubar (preposition 'over, above, across, beyond') and ubiri (adverb), from Proto-Germanic *uberi (cognate with English 'over', Gothic ufar), from Proto-Indo-European *upéri ('over, above', comparative of *upó, cf. Latin super, Ancient Greek hypér).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): über
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): über

überall.etymology: From Middle High German über al and Old High German ubar al ('over everything, without exception, everywhere'), univerbation of the prepositional phrase über ('over') + accusative neuter singular al ('all, everything').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): überall
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): überall

übergang.etymology: Continues Middle High German überganc ('going across, crossing, transition'), formed from über ('over, across', OHG ubar) and Gang ('walk, passage, movement', verbal noun of gehen).

rootFamily.gloss: to pass over into, blend into

übergang.notes: In music, der Übergang is the bridge passage that connects one section or key smoothly into the next.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Übergang
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Übergang

übergeben.etymology: From Middle High German übergeben ('to hand over, surrender, deliver; reflexively: to vomit'), prefix verb combining über- ('over, across') and geben ('to give', OHG geban); the reflexive sense 'to vomit' arose as a euphemism ('to give oneself over / bring up').

history.meaning: to hand over, surrender, give up

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): übergeben
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): übergeben

überhaupt.etymology: From Middle High German über houbet ('in the aggregate, altogether, in general, at all'), originally a livestock trading expression meaning 'buying a herd by the total count without pricing each head of cattle (Haupt) individually', later generalized to 'in general, at all'.

history.meaning: without counting individual heads, as a whole

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): überhaupt
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): überhaupt

überlassen.etymology: From Middle High German überlāzen ('to leave over, hand over, relinquish, entrust to someone'), prefix verb combining über- ('over') and lassen ('to let, leave', OHG lāzan).

history.meaning: to leave or hand over to someone

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): überlassen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): überlassen

überleben.etymology: From Middle High German überleben and Old High German ubarlebēn ('to outlive, live beyond, survive'), inseparable prefix verb combining über- ('beyond, past') and leben ('to live', OHG lebēn), parallel to Latin supervivere.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): überleben
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): überleben

übernehmen.etymology: From Middle High German übernemen ('to take over, assume responsibility for, undertake; reflexively: to overexert oneself'), prefix verb combining über- ('over') and nehmen ('to take', OHG neman).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): übernehmen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): übernehmen

überreichen.etymology: Formed from the prefix 'über-' (over, across) and 'reichen' (to hand, reach). The base verb comes from the Proto-Germanic *raikijaną. The compound describes formally handing something over to another person. It implies a sense of ceremony or respect not present in simple 'geben'.
überreichen.notes: Inseparable verb, unlike many others with 'über-'.

sources.title: DWDS
Wiktionary

überstehen.etymology: From Middle High German überstēn, überstān and Old High German ubarstān ('to stand through to the end, endure, weather, survive; as a separable verb: to jut out, protrude'), combining über- ('through, over') and stehen ('to stand', OHG stān).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): überstehen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): überstehen

übrig.etymology: From Middle High German überec, überic ('remaining over, left over, superfluous'), derived with suffix -ig from über ('over, beyond', OHG ubar).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): übrig
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): übrig

übrigens.etymology: 17th-century Early New High German adverbial formation built on the adjective übrig ('left over, remaining', MHG überec, from über 'over') with the weak inflectional stem -en- plus adverbial genitive -s, paralleling übrigens' older prepositional phrase im Übrigen ('for the rest, besides').

morphemes.meaning: weak genitive adverbial ending (cf. erstens, mindestens)

history.meaning: for the rest, moreover, by the way (17th c.)

cognates.meaning: by the way, moreover (exact structural match)
cognate with the base root über-

übrigens.notes: Evolved from 'as for what remains unsaid' into the standard conversational discourse marker 'by the way / incidentally'.
